speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I spoke too hastily on Friday last when I implied that under the previous government there had been no delays in holding by-elections which had the effect of depriving constituencies of representation for the whole of a session of parliament. I do not want to leave this misinformation uncorrected.
I find there were several cases both before the 1953 general election and the 1957 general election when by-elections were not called, apparently because it was common knowledge that a general election was approaching. But there were two other cases where there was no such extenuating circumstance. The Prime Minister reminded me that Brandon-Souris became vacant late in 1950 and the by-election was not held until June of 1951. That also happened in one of the seats in Queens, Prince Edward Island, at the same time. I doubt whether either of these precedents would commend itself to the government, since in both cases members of the opposition were elected and both members then elected are today ministers of the crown.
In expressing my regret to the house for having misinformed hon. members may I also thank the Prime Minister for the assurance that there will no longer be any similar delays in the calling of by-elections.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege with reference to a Canadian Press dispatch reporting an address I delivered to graduate students at the Ontario Agricultural College in Guelph last Friday night. In the first paragraph of this dispatch, which appeared in a number of morning and evening newspapers on Saturday, I am reported to have said that future immigration into Canada would be "limited to persons with a craft, skill or profession".
This paragraph, in which I was incorrectly reported, was subsequently corrected in two later Canadian Press leads, but unfortunately the original story received such widespread circulation that I feel it necessary to set the record straight. The text of my Guelph address is available to the public. I was speaking of the effects of the technological revolution on Canadian agriculture and industry. What I said was quite clear, and I quote:
We certainly shall have to do everything within our power to make it clear to everyone, and especially to our young people, that there is going to be little room for the unskilled or the half-skilled worker in the world of tomorrow. It ought to be quite clear to everybody that employment opportunities-for native Canadians as well as immigrants-are going to be limited in future for people without some kind of trade, skill or profession.
There was nothing in my Guelph speech suggesting that immigration would be restricted to those with skills and trades.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would be entertaining and amusing, if it were not so serious, to study in detail the extent to which the Prime Minister and the members of the government have gone to make the people of Canada believe that the Conservatives are whistling the same tune today that they whistled so melodiously in 1957. One can barely recall- the picture is fading very rapidly-the selfassurance and even the overconfidence of the Prime Minister when he marched across the country all but submerged in the solutions he professed to have to all the problems, national and international. Among other things he led Canadians to believe that he had found the formula to increase social legislation, reduce taxes and balance the budget. Of course no one would suffer from unemployment, not while the Prime Minister was administering the affairs of Canada.
His predictions also contained a very vivid description of the Conservative vision of utopian Canada where full employment would be the order of the day, where our economy would be stabilized and tight money unheard of, where our national defence would be adequately provided for and our trade deficits would be brought into balance. This was the type of tune whistled in 1957 by the Conservatives.
The tune began to change immediately on their taking office. Instead of the self-assured, confident Billy Graham the Canadians had listened to, the Canadian people found that they had elected a very surprised Prime Minister leading an unprepared and bewildered government in the uncompromising intricacies of government administration without any notion whatever as to how they were going to implement any of the promises they had made, let alone how they were going to achieve anything remotely resembling the utopian vision of Canada under a Conservative administration.
The government's first tactic was then to appear to be busy and to be accomplishing things, and a great deal of publicity was given to the Prime Minister's travels abroad and around the world; and the government's statement with respect to a 15 per cent diversion of trade from the United States to the United Kingdom was made on the basis of sensationalism rather than on the basis of the wisdom and soundness of the action involved.
The description by the Minister of Finance of the commonwealth trade conference, which he claimed was a colossal success, can be justified only in terms of propaganda, because that particular trade conference will forever

Dominion-Provincial Relations haunt the minister for having refused to accept the offer of a reciprocal free trade area with the United Kingdom. Smoke screen propaganda was the first Conservative tactic employed to camouflage the government's lack of over-all policies.
Then the government resorted to the inheritance tactic, by which means it sought to justify its inaction on the ground that it had inherited its administrative problems from the previous Liberal government, conveniently forgetting, of course, that these were the very problems the Conservatives in 1957 promised to solve.
Next the government tried the naive approach, the "what recession?" and the "what unemployment problem?" approach. When the opposition pointed out the very real dangers to our economy of an ever-increasing number of unemployed the government immediately turned to the "prophets of doom and gloom" and "selling Canada short" tactics. Whenever I hear hon. members opposite criticizing the Liberal opposition and accusing them of undermining the people's confidence in Canada because we dare criticize the government's inaction and lack of policies, I cannot help but recall a certain premier of Quebec who finally convinced himself that he was the province of Quebec. Surely the Prime Minister and members of the government, after so short a term in office, do not now already identify themselves with Canada. Surely the Prime Minister and the members of the government know and understand that Canadians can have-and indeed a number of Canadians do have-a considerable amount of confidence in Canada but no confidence in the government.
The current tactic, of course, is particularly interesting because it is so revealing. It is not as cunning or as imaginative as the other tactics. It is a tactic in which are employed expression of confusion, bewilderment, and exasperation. Perhaps it could be characterized as the "what would you do?" tactic. This tactic, of course, is already burnt out because on all the national urgent problems the Liberal opposition has stated what it would do, to the great discomfort of the government.
Oh, oh.

Of course, Mr. Speaker, hon. members opposite do not have any intention of taking up these suggestions. They prefer to ignore them. However, if the Conservatives really want to find out what the Liberals would do, let the government call an election and we shall be happy to show them.
Oh, oh.

Many people unfortunately not only consider as smart politics the tactics I


have just described, but unfortunately they accept these practices as normal political procedure. I believe-and I feel very strongly about this-that there is no surer way of undermining and indeed destroying the people's confidence in our political system and in our democratic form of government than by the use by a political party, whatever its denomination, of tactics whose aim is primarily to enhance and preserve its political prestige but whose consequences are to mislead and confuse the public on vital urgent national issues so that objective analysis of the problem becomes impossible. Extremely urgent fundamental problems become insoluble simply because the effective solutions might prove unpopular to one or more classes of our social structure; and so as not to jeopardize its popularity, the party merely ignores the solution and jeopardizes the economy instead. Such tactics are not only small politics but are an indescribable injustice to the people who have not only a right but a responsibility to be aware of, to understand and to judge national problems as they really are and not as one political party would like to pretend they are.
The greatest proof that such tactics are not to be taken for smart politics is that in spite of the torrent of words the members of the government have uttered in implementing their successive strategies, none of the urgent problems have been solved and some indeed have become more serious.
Of all the problems facing the government which have not yet been solved I doubt if there is a more fundamental, important, complex or urgent one than that of federal-provincial relations and federal tax-sharing, arrangements.
Oh, oh.
I hope that hon. members opposite are not laughing at the problems involved in federal-provincial relations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are laughing at the hon. member.

Apparently the proposals made by the Prime Minister in October can be described as laughing at the problems involved in provincial-federal relations. The federal-provincial tax-sharing agreement criticized so violently by the Conservatives expires in March of 1962, and new fiscal arrangements will have to be provided during this session of parliament as announced in the speech from the throne. Perhaps it might be very timely now to examine a statement made by the Prime Minister in 1957, as reported by the Canadian Press on April 26 of that year:
Mr. Diefenbaker pledged to work out new taxsharing arrangements with the provinces which

would strengthen Canada's federal system and give provinces and municipalities the funds to carry their responsibilities.
He said:
A Conservative government, if elected, would immediately call a federal-provincial conference to settle existing problems. The federal system was threatened by "the centralization complex of the St. Laurent government" and a healthy balance [DOT]of revenues between federal and provincial governments must be assured.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister [DOT]does not dare to claim that so far he has fulfilled that promise. And how can the Prime Minister now condone and accept, as he is doing, the Liberal principles and the basis on which fiscal arrangements with the provinces were achieved if indeed they were a threat to the federal system, as he claimed they were in 1957? And if they are not a threat, on what grounds can the Prime Minister justify so insidious an accusation on a matter as fundamentally important as federal-provincial relations, an accusation which in fact did undermine the people's confidence in our federal system.
There have been few issues indeed that have been given the Conservative political football treatment more mercilessly than the fundamental and extremely difficult problem of federal-provincial relations. This may gain votes for the Conservative party, but it has not only confused the thinking of Canadians but has made an already difficult problem almost incomprehensible and retarded and jeopardized the progress that has been made so far toward an equitable solution to this extremely urgent problem.
It is only now that Canadians realize that the Conservative accusations were unfounded and unjustified, and that the present fiscal arrangements with the provinces, though admittedly not an ideal solution, were in fact a serious and sound approach to the problem. The government, instead of rejecting the substance of the fiscal arrangements which they criticized so violently, are now speaking of the difficulties and the problems involved which make any alternative solution to those arrangements extremely difficult. The Conservatives, of course, did not speak of those problems nor those difficulties when they were discussing federal-provincial relations in 1957. At that time they were merely content to confuse the issue.
Federal-provincial relations did not arise only with the Rowell-Sirois report of 1940; they were born with confederation. The provinces at that time saw the advantages to be derived by them in a federal system, and it is impossible to conceive that the fundamental principle of confederation could have been based on anything else than on co-operation and understanding between the autonomous
Dominion-Provincial Relations provinces and the federal government. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that at no time has that principle ever been broken, and that taxsharing arrangements have indeed been an application of that principle.
The exigencies of the war, the demand and urgent need for social legislation, the disparity in the financial resources of the different provinces, the justifiable desire to achieve uniformity in social aid, in the standards of living and in national unity, coupled with the increasing financial demands made within the rapidly expanding provinces and municipalities, presented problems which the fathers of confederation could never have dreamed of and for which they did not adequately provide in the constitution or in the methods of taxation made available to the provinces and to the federal government.
The urgency of the problems, both provincial and federal, and the fact that no clear-cut solution to these problems could be found within the framework of the constitution, made it necessary to resort to the principle of co-operation between the federal government and the provinces to find some alternative solution. That alternative solution was found, Mr. Speaker, when Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent introduced the tax-sharing arrangements which were so violently criticized by the Conservatives.
It would be useful, I think, to review the provisions of those tax-sharing agreements which, in 1957, the Prime Minister felt were a threat to the federal system. Hon. members will recall that under these agreements, first of all, the provinces were completely free to rent their rights to direct taxation or to levy their own direct taxes and have them collected by the federal government, or, third, to levy and collect their direct taxes without interference.
Second, by this agreement the provinces were enabled to derive more than 20 per cent of urgently needed additional revenues during the first years of the new arrangements as compared with the previous years without imposing double taxation and this percentage, of course, increased substantially in succeeding years.
Third, equalization payments based on the tax yield of the two wealthiest provinces were provided to enable the less wealthy provinces to face their constitutional responsibilities. Such an interprovincial redistribution of revenue, as I said before, is essential to preserve a proper balance within our federal system.
Finally, stabilization payments were offered to the provinces as a guarantee against any

Dominion-Provincial Relations material decline in revenues from the direct tax field that could result from a prolonged recession.
These 1957 fiscal arrangements, Mr. Speaker, were financially advantageous to the provinces. They completely respected the constitutional rights of the provinces and provided to them, especially to the less wealthy provinces, substantially more revenue without double taxation. We do not claim, nor did Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent ever claim, that these arrangements were the ideal, the complete or the final solution of the federal-provincial problems. But, Mr. Speaker, they did permit both the federal government and the provinces to hurdle what could have become economic and financial disasters in either or both levels of government. And this was done without any of the provinces losing one iota of their sovereignty or autonomy.
It was within the responsibility and the prerogative of the federal government, with the co-operation and authorization of the provinces, to provide the much needed social measures on a uniform basis throughout the country at a time when the economy of most of the provinces could not afford the expenses involved. It has always been the accepted role of the federal government to supply public services which could not be supplied by other levels of government or by private enterprise; but, Mr. Speaker, if the provinces feel they are now ready to assume the responsibility of implementing some of the social measures presenty carried out by the federal government and can guarantee that these measures will continue to be uniform to Canadians in all provinces, then a redistribution of responsibilities as well as of taxes could be considered as the basis of new tax agreements. But the problem has always been whether the provinces could or would add additional responsibilities to their problems of rapid expansion, and whether some uniformity of social legislation would be maintained in all provinces.
A Liberal government, Mr. Speaker, would not object to withdrawing from joint federal-provincial schemes which are now firmly established in the provinces and which the provinces felt they could administer themselves, such as was suggested by the premier of Quebec to the conference in July. To my mind it is part of the federal government's role to co-operate with the provinces in implementing needed legislation and to withdraw when the provinces feel they can carry on alone, but it will be noted that this is the first time a provincial premier has formally expressed his willingness to assume additional financial responsibilities in compensation for additional revenues, and this may

well be the key that might open the door to better federal-provincial relations.
In 1957 the Prime Minister waxed eloquent on the supposedly arrogant attitude of the Liberal government in its dealings with the provinces. In his opening campaign speech in Massey hall, Toronto, on April 25, 1957 he said:
We intend to form a government to immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference to bring about a settlement of these problems, not in the spirit of arrogant domination as displayed by the present government but in the spirit of unity and amity and with mutual tolerance and respect.
He repeated this statement from coast to coast. We shall see, Mr. Speaker, whether the Prime Minister really kept his promises. After the 1957 election a federal-provincial conference was held but was reluctantly convened. It was not convened immediately but in November, 1957. The purpose of the conference was not to bring about a statement of the problem but to get to know one another, and fiscal arrangements were hardly discussed at that particular conference.
Second, it had been agreed at the November conference that there would be a further conference held in the early part of 1958; but the government, in a spirit of amity and tolerance but without consulting the provinces, replaced the conference by a telegram sent to all the provinces containing erroneous calculations made not by the Department of Finance but by Mr. George Gathercole, a top civil servant of the Ontario government.
Third, the Minister of Finance in his brisk and supposedly efficient manner set up a committee on finance consisting of the Minister of Finance and the provincial treasurers to reconsider fiscal problems, and more particularly to consider the request made by the provinces to have the 1957 arrangements revised. The committee met in July and in October of 1959. At this last meeting the Minister of Finance, ignoring the insistent request of the provinces and ignoring the Conservative promises of 1957, amicably announced that the tax-sharing arrangements would not be modified.

Dominion-Provincial Relations

You will have an opportunity to debate the question. Surely the Prime Minister is not serious when he claims to have carried out his formal pledge to bring about a settlement of federal-provincial relations, not in a spirit of arrogant domination but in a spirit of unity, amity and with mutual tolerance and respect, when his inaction and his attitude under the circumstances can be described not only as arrogant but as downright insulting to the provinces. But perhaps the greatest breach of the Prime Minister's pledge to settle the problem of federal-provincial relations, and indeed the greatest insult to the provinces, is that the government, in spite of its promises, has evidently after three and a half years not taken the trouble to analyse, study and understand the problems involved in the field of federal-provincial relations. A review of the government's statements at each of the federal-provincial conferences indicates clearly that the government has no over-all plan to solve this problem, and is indeed completely unprepared to negotiate with the provinces.
I would strongly advise the government, Mr. Speaker, not to try to tackle the problem of federal-provincial relations with an ill thought out and off the cuff solution such as the suggestion the Prime Minister made to the provinces at the conference in October. If the government imposes on the provinces the proposal he made at that time they will not only repudiate the magnanimous attitude the Prime Minister displayed in 1957, but they will destroy the basic principles upon which better and sounder federal-provincial relations can be continued.
At a press conference in Winnipeg on May 14, 1957, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of that date, the present Prime Minister stated:
The first thing a Conservative government would .do, he said, would be to call a federal-provincial conference which would be held 'in the spirit of confederation' to arrive at a tax rental formula 'more in keeping with the needs of the provinces and municipalities'.
Under recent tax agreements, he said, the provinces have been forced to a 'starved condition'. Municipalities have been placed in a position where property owners are saddled with heavy burden Qf taxation.
He charged that continued centralization of *taxation by the federal government was leaving the municipalities as 'the forgotten people'.
Present tax relations, Mr. Diefenbaker maintained, are a 'haphazard outgrowth' of wartime agreements which don't meet the problems of Canada today. The federal government offered 'cut and dried' plans which the provinces had to accept.
Under a Conservative government, he said, the provinces would have a voice in deciding fiscal terms and the tax agreements would contribute -to national unity.


These indeed, Mr. Speaker, are noble words and noble sentiments, but it is most unfortunate that none of these noble sentiments have been reflected in the least in the proposals the Prime Minister made to the provinces last October. The proposals the Prime Minister made to the provinces in October contain these features:
1.	The federal tax rates in the three shared tax fields would be reduced by the amount of the present standard rates, that is 14, 9 and 50. This proposal has two implications. First, the federal government is not prepared to vacate any additional field of direct taxation in order to enable the provinces to get more revenues from direct taxes without adding to the over-all tax burden. Second, all the provinces will have to levy and collect their direct taxes, as some of them are doing now under the provisions of the present arrangements. The provinces will not be able to make tax rental or tax collection agreements with the federal government as they do now. This would mean that all Canadian taxpayers would have to file two income tax returns, and it would also mean additional costs to the provinces for the collection of taxes.
2.	Federal subsidies, fixed at $220 million per year, would be distributed amongst the provinces to take the place of the present equalization payments, the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and the special grants to Newfoundland under section 2 of the Newfoundland Additional Grants Act. A new but unspecified formula of distribution of those grants would replace the present one which is based on the average yield of standard direct tax rates in the top two provinces. This represents, in my opinion, a clear repudiation of the equalization principle which the Prime Minister had promised in July to maintain. I shall return to that point later.
3.	Stabilization payments would be based on the yield of the standard taxes in the last two years of the current arrangements, that is in 1960-61 and 1961-62. At present those payments are determined on a moving basis and are based for any one year on tax yields of the two previous years. The change proposed by the federal government means, for all practical purposes, the abandonment of the stabilization principle unless we experience an acute depression in Canada during the next few years.
4.	Reciprocal application of sales and commodity taxes to federal and provincial crown agencies would be provided, but no material changes are proposed with respect to conditional grant and shared cost arrangements.
5.	The use of sales taxes at the retail level by the provinces would be confirmed through

an amendment to the British North America Act. Such a proposal, Mr. Speaker, has very little significance in terms of additional provincial revenues, since all provinces can even now levy such taxes. As a matter of fact seven provinces already do so.
There is, however, one redeeming feature of the Prime Minister's proposals, Mr. Speaker. It is that the federal government has succeeded finally in creating unanimity amongst the provinces. They were unanimously and vehemently against the federal proposals. The Toronto Star of October 27 gave a very succinct and very accurate description of the feeling of the 10 premiers. The headline reads "10 Premiers Turn Thumbs Down on P.M. Offer". In commenting on the proposals this is what the different premiers had to say:
Robiehaud, New Brunswick: Preposterous.
Stanfield, Nova Scotia:	No better off.
Roblin, Manitoba: No good.
Smallwood, Newfoundland: Disillusioned.
Frost, Ontario: Meaningless.
Bennett, British Columbia: Unrealistic.
Shaw, Prince Edward Island: Not in favour.
Douglas, Saskatchewan: Retrograde.
Manning, Alberta: Deceptive.
Lesage, Quebec: Unacceptable.

Dominion-Provincial Relations criticized the Liberal government for taking too large a share of the joint field of direct taxes, thus forcing the provinces into a starved condition. What has this government done, Mr. Speaker? In 1958 the present government increased the provincial share of personal income tax by 3 per cent of the federal rate. But in 1959 the federal government increased its own share of the corporate income tax by an additional 3 per cent tax on profits. I should like to emphasize this point, that the federal share of the joint field of direct taxes is higher in 1960-61 than it would have been in 1957-58 under the provisions of Mr. Harris' budgetary proposals.
Moreover, the present government does not propose to vacate the field of direct taxation any further during the next five years. It has pushed its tax rates as high as it can and now refuses to provide any additional leeway in order to enable the provinces to exercise their rights without adding to an already heavy tax burden. In fact this government asserts that its fiscal needs have a priority over provincial financial requirements.
This refusal to provide additional room for provincial taxes must be related to equalization in order to understand fully what it means to the provinces. As I said before, the federal government, in spite of the firm commitment made by the Prime Minister in July, 1960, now proposes to abandon the principle of equalization and to distribute an unvarying amount of money each year to the provinces. This proposal, Mr. Speaker, I submit is most unfair to most provinces.
This proposal means that the few rich provinces having high tax yields will continue, as at present, to benefit from those increasing yields, but the other provinces will not be able to share further in the country's prosperity. In other words, all provinces except one will be worse off under the new proposal than they would be if the existing arrangements had been simply continued. An undesirable but increasing differential in per capita tax revenue will develop among provinces, and this differential is likely to increase rapidly for another reason. The provinces have been told by the federal government to increase their own direct tax rates if they want more revenues. This procedure might be a possible solution for those few provinces which have a high tax potential, but it will not be possible for most provinces.
We all know, of course, that direct tax yields, and especially the per capita yields from corporate income tax, vary from one province to another. This fact is clearly shown in a table presented by the Minister of Finance last year, which table appears at page

Dominion-Provincial Relations 2230 of Hansard of that year. This table indicates that corporate income tax of 1 per cent would yield per capita in the current fiscal year $2.64 in Ontario, $2.18 in British Columbia, $2.05 in Alberta, $1.97 in Quebec, $1.56 in Manitoba, $1.13 in Saskatchewan, $1.02 in Nova Scotia, 88 cents in New Brunswick, 79 cents in Newfoundland and 54 cents in Prince Edward Island.
As we can see, the per capita yield of such a tax in Prince Edward Island is only 20 per cent of what it is in Ontario. On the basis of a 1 per cent corporation income tax, without equalization, Quebec, for instance, would lose almost $3J million in revenue as compared with Ontario. In order to get the same per capita revenue that Ontario receives from a 1 per cent corporate income tax, Prince Edward Island would have to levy a tax of 5 per cent and Newfoundland would have to impose a tax of 3 J per cent. This comparison indicates how inequitable the federal proposal is when it requires the provinces from now on to finance any addition to their services from their own taxes, without equalization.
For certain provinces, at least, the constitutional power of direct taxation is almost only theoretical; in practice it cannot be used to provide adequate provincial revenues. What will happen, Mr. Speaker, in those provinces as provincial financial requirements increase, under the Conservative proposal which would force the provinces to increase their own taxes without equalization? Those provinces would have to impose prohibitive rates of taxes, or refuse needed improvements in provincial services, or ask the federal government to take over their constitutional responsibilities. None of those solutions is compatible with fairness and the proper balance of our federal system.
In summary, the federal government tells the provinces "We will freeze and maintain the benefits you receive under the tax-sharing arrangements negotiated by the Liberals, but you will not get anything more in the future from a Conservative government". As the Leader of the Opposition stated in Sussex on October 29, by driving the provinces back into double taxation and by refusing to apply in the future the principles of equalization and stabilization, the present government is proposing to undo the progress made in federal-provincial fiscal relations and to return the provinces to the financial strait jacket they were in during the days of R. B. Bennett. From now on, as in the early thirties, all the provinces will be left alone to face their increasing financial responsibilities. This situation is exactly what produced so much inequality among the provinces in the early thirties and caused the acute crisis of our

federal system which was so vividly described in the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission in 1940.
The Liberal party is strongly opposed to the proposal made by the government to the provinces last October. We believe that the basic features of the existing tax-sharing arrangements should be maintained. We also believe that they can be improved in certain respects not by going backward, as the government proposes to do, but by moving forward.
Without going into the details of this complex question, may I say that the general attitude of the Liberal party in this field can be summarized by the following propositions:
1.	We believe in regular consultation with the provinces in order to ensure that priorities in the use of taxes are kept constantly in line with changing conditions and in order to ensure that the provincial governments have adequate revenues with which to provide for their citizens and adequate standard of services and to perform their constitutional obligations. Another important new area for co-operation is in the borrowing operations of municipal, provincial and federal authorities. More regular consultation and closer co-operation require the creation of a permanent federal-provincial secretariat.
2.	We believe that the principle of equalization should be strengthened instead of being abandoned, and that all provinces should receive the same revenue, per head of population, from the direct taxes shared with the federal government. In this way Canadians everywhere would receive an equal share of tax revenues derived from national economic activities and all provinces would be in a better position to face by themselves their constitutional responsibilities.
3.	The principle of stabilization should also be retained and strengthened. Tax revenues fall off if we encounter a serious recession, but there is no lessening of the need for roads, schools and other services provided by the provinces and the municipalities. Stabilization payments in any given year should be related to the revenues of the previous year.
4.	We believe that the permanent programs which had to be started on a shared cost basis by federal and provincial governments and which are now firmly established throughout Canada should be left entirely to the provinces, and that the federal government should evolve appropriate readjustments in its taxes so as to provide for full provincial financing of those programs.
5.	Finally, we believe that adjustment grants should be available on a basis of a formula

which could be applied to any part of the country, for any province in special fiscal need.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are some of the proposals that we feel should be offered to the provinces and be embodied in the new tax-sharing arrangements. Mr. Speaker, today we are debating a topic that is very complex indeed. At this time I should like to express the opinion of this group. We intend to support the amendment offered by the official opposition, but in our opinion it is inadequate. It asks only for a continuation in principle of existing arrangements, and does not call for an extension of the basic principle underlying existing do-monion-provincial tax-sharing arrangements. Our amendment to the amendment of the Liberals is going to attempt to underline the need for an extension of the underlying basic principles of these agreements.
In 1867 the fathers of confederation reached an agreement whereby responsibilities and powers of taxation as between the two levels of government were arrived at, and we had emerge the British North America Act. At that time the builders of the Canadian nation, meeting in Prince Edward Island, were unable to see how in the years ahead the responsibilities of our provincial governments were going to grow by leaps and bounds. They also failed to see how in years to come we would have a condition wherein new responsibilities would have to be assumed in the main by our other levels of government and that the revenues of the national government would increase at the same time.
For years the problem has been met, in part at least, by the federal government increasingly assuming a partnership role with the other levels of government. Each year we note how the federal government is in many ways attempting to share the responsibility that was imposed upon the provincial governments by the terms of the British North America Act. Already this session we have had legislation before us under which the federal government will attempt to help
Dominion-Provincial Relations the other level of government in the field of education. There has been a growth in federal participation in the meeting of these new and larger responsibilities that the lower levels of government now have.
The other method devised some years ago was one whereby the provinces agreed to rent out to the federal government certain taxation rights in return for revenue from the federal treasury. We had evolved the taxsharing agreements. There has been a lot of misunderstanding in this matter. The federal government has attempted to assume its fair share of the problems of government. Whenever the federal government has moved in to assist the other level of government in such matters as education, highways, health and welfare and unemployment, there have been protests as to the terms and even as to the basic essence of the tax-sharing agreements that have been arrived at. Obviously the easy solution is that about which we have read and heard much, the return to the provinces of their basic rights to tax in order to enable them to look after their constitutional responsibilities.
That is an easy answer, but it does not resolve the basic problem. It is the attitude of Pontius Pilate washing his hands when faced with a difficult decision. In effect, this latest move in October last whereby the federal government offered to return to the provinces their right in the matter of direct taxation was an adoption of the position of Pontius Pilate, the federal government attempting to wash its hands of a problem at a time when we face grave responsibilities in this regard. I submit that the answer is not easy. However, I also submit that the answer will not be arrived at by unloading the whole problem on to the necks of all provincial governments.
This last move, if it were to be accepted by our provincial governments, has in it implications that we all ought to be aware of. There is a danger, because if the provinces accepted this last offer of the federal government we would have a national government that would find itself unable to deal with problems of recession and depression. It would find itself completely handicapped in dealing with the very difficult problem of unemployment. The national government would find itself in a position where it was completely prevented from lending any effective hand in the matter of national development. It would accentuate the inequalities that exist between the standards of living of Canadians in various provinces of Canada. They would have made no contribution toward resolving the very severe handicap under which our municipalities must now operate. Were this proposal

Dominion-Provincial Relations accepted the national government would immediately realize that it would be completely unable henceforth to assist in the matter of education. It would also find itself unable to resolve problems of regional handicaps under which so many of our Canadian people suffer.
We find, therefore, because of all the dangers involved, that the offer of the government to the provinces is not in the interests of our nation. We realize, of course, that there is a problem, as I said before, and we have been given many assurances. I have looked at the Conservative promises made during the last election, as they are to be found in the compilation that has been referred to so often in this house. I notice that hardly any subject contains so many pledges and so many promises on the part of the then leader of the Conservative party, now the Prime Minister, as this matter of dominion-provincial taxation arrangements, or their fiscal arrangements. There are pages and pages of pledges that were given by the then leader of the Conservative party. In reading through all of them one finds that certainly there is no indication that the Conservatives intended to abdicate their responsibilities in this regard.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And they have never done so.

In our opinion this latest move of theirs is an abdication of their responsibilities as leaders of our nation. They are intending to throw the difficult situation into the laps of the provinces. We feel that this is completely inadequate, and is exactly the opposite of the essence of their promises made to the Canadian people at that time.
I might simply touch on the matter of interest rates that other levels of governments have to pay. I refer to the Victoria Times of May 22, 1957, where we find that the man who is now our Prime Minister had, this to say, and it, is in quotation marks:
Even the city of Victoria has to pay outrageous rates of interest today.
Again, in his home town of Prince Albert, as reported in the Prince Albert Herald of May 28, 1957, the Prime Minister said:
Prince Albert knows when it borrows that it has to pay an exorbitant rate of interest to the east.
Yet now, if the offer of the government were to be accepted, there would be no possibility of any help on the part of this government, with all the resources at its command, toward relieving the interest burdens that have to be borne by our provinces and municipalities. As a matter of fact, only recently in the baby budget the minister imposed an even higher rate of interest on our

municipalities and our provincial governments, and it is nonsense that our provinces have to be-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member is now speaking about the budget. The statement he has made about the budget is completely untrue. I take it, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the proper place or time to be discussing the budget. We have had the budget debate.

Mr. Speaker, on the point of order raised by the minister, I wonder whether Your Honour would consider enforcing the rules on the minister as well as on the other members of the house and prevent him from raising these phony points of order which enable him to reply to arguments in debate.

On the point of order, the rate that has to be paid by the provincial governments is very much a part of the financial arrangements or, in my submission at least, it ought to be a part of the financial arrangements arrived at between the national government and our provincial governments. I therefore feel, even though there was a reference in the budget to those interest rates and to the borrowings of provincial governments, it is also very much an integral part of the debate now before us. I note in the report-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I rule on the point of order. Of course in my mind the subject matter of the amendment moved by the hon. member seems to me to be somewhat restricted, because it brings into discussion only the principle of equalization of direct tax revenues as they exist today, compared with the proposal made at the last federal-provincial conference, which would freeze them, if my interpretation is correct.
It is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member knows what I mean. Therefore I do not think it would be appropriate to discuss the whole financial situation of the federal government or even the whole problem of fiscal arrangements with the provinces. Unless I misinterpret the amendment, this is the way I feel the discussion should be limited.

I realized, Mr. Speaker, that I might have a little difficulty and I did discuss with a number of members the possible limitations of the debate now going on. However, this very matter of the proposal of the government to freeze the incomes, or the possible incomes, of our provincial governments raises, at least to a certain degree, the effect of this limitation of

the incomes of our provinces. It was for that reason that I brought in the matter of interest rates although I had not intended to pursue it, Mr. Speaker.
It is our contention that dominion-provincial fiscal relations-and I should like to endorse what the Liberal spokesman had to say on this point-ought to be a continuing process; that a permanent organization should be established whereby the growing problems of the two levels of government could be a matter of continuing discussion. I should like to underline his call for the establishment of a dominion-provincial secretariat wherein the minister of this government would preside over continuous meetings with representatives of each of the ten provinces, which would co-ordinate our problems as they have arisen and will continue to arise. We feel that a continuation of the equalization principle is essential in order to give Canadians in all parts of Canada equal opportunities, in order to enable the government to continue to exercise control over the welfare of the national economy.
The proposal of the government would in fact establish within the borders of Canada ten different Canadian nations, and we believe that would be most regrettable. We would find people in Nova Scotia becoming poorer and poorer while other provinces would continue to become wealthier and wealthier. Equal opportunities for all Canadians would then fly out the window. We need a national government that is able to use ways and means to assure to as great extent as is constitutionally possible equal opportunities for all Canadians in all parts of Canada. We also need a continuation of the basic equalization principle in order to enable the national government to exercise a policy of selective development in those areas of Canada where development is most urgently needed.
We also urge a continuation of this principle in order that at least a little more progress can be made toward helping our municipalities meet their growing responsibilities. We have to recognize the need to share our responsibilities no matter where we live in Canada, and the proposal of the government to hand back to the provinces direct powers of taxation would mean nothing more or less than that the wealthier provinces would be enabled thereby to get off the hook of carrying out as Canadians their share of responsibility to those Canadians living in less privileged areas. We do not want to see a return to the provinces of the right to levy their own income taxes. We believe this would bring in its wake many evil results.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
In the new agreements that we hope will be arrived at we should also like to see, in addition to the continuation of the equalization principle, ways and means devised whereby in effect there will not be a penalty imposed on those provinces that desire to be progressive and which introduce legislation of various kinds that other provinces may be years in initiating. What I have in mind particularly is that if a province wants to embark on a prepaid medical care program, ways and means ought to be found whereby that province is not going to be penalized indirectly in the years to come for having undertaken a progressive measure albeit ahead of the rest of the provinces. I have in mind such things as the Trans-Canada Highway Act and a national health insurance plan.
We believe that in addition to the equalization principle the tax-sharing arrangements proposed by the government should embody a new principle, a sharing of the problem of raising the necessary social capital. The federal government has under its control the Bank of Canada, and we feel that our municipalities and provinces should be helped, that the time is overdue for the government to come to the aid of other levels of government in the matter of helping to meet their capital needs.
We also do not like the proposal of the Prime Minister that the existing amount of revenue available for equalization will henceforth be taken and allotted to the provinces. It is our view that by doing so we are getting away from the basic principle into the realm of a Santa Claus prime minister deciding when and how and to which of the provinces he is going to pay additional allowances. I know we already have arrangements whereby we pay additional allowances to certain provinces, but we do not like the abolition of agreements that are based on fundamental principles and the instituting of grants instead whereby the government, according to its whim of the moment, would be able to make what in effect would be hand-outs to what it considered to be needy provinces.
We might thus return to a situation where, if the political complexion of a particular provincial government did not meet with the approval of the government of Canada, the province in question would then be discriminated against. We might again have the five-cent speech of Mackenzie King in the annals of Canadian history; that is to say, unless the people of this province vote into office a provincial government of my liking I can assure them they will not get a nickel out of the national government.

Dominion-Provincial Relations This would be a return to the days of Mr. Duplessis, who decided on his own hook to which parishes he was going to give grants for educational purposes. I am very happy that the new government in the province of Quebec intends, if it has not already done so, to remove this inequity and to enact legislation whereby the parishes will have the right to obtain school grants. We want our provincial governments and the people of Canada to have the right to equal opportunities. We do not want them to have that right only at the pleasure of whoever happens to be prime minister at any particular time in our history.
So far as this matter is concerned, I believe we in Canada have to operate as a team. Let us have a united Canada with a national government working in co-operation with the ten provincial governments. I hope we can end the political competition that has too often been evident in relations between the two levels of government and between particular provinces and the national government. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That the amendment be amended by inserting after the word "resolved" in the first line of paragraph 2, "(a)", and adding to the proposed amendment the following subparagraph:
"(b) and be it further resolved that this house is of the opinion that the present tax-sharing agreements should be extended to provide sufficient federal assistance to the provinces so as to enable them to assist the municipalities in the provision of essential capital services."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before I put the
amendment, would any hon. member care to comment as to its admissibility? I should like to have the guidance of hon. members.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether you wish an observation on that point. I think it is quite obvious that this would involve a substantial charge upon the crown, and it may well go outside the scope of the original amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should like to have the views of the house in connection with citation 202 in Beauchesne's fourth edition, paragraph 3. Reference may be made also to May, page 421, in connection with the relevancy of amendments. My worry is that the amendment deals only with the principle involved in equalization payments, which is something quite different from the tax-sharing arrangements. It would seem, therefore, that the subamendment would widen the scope of the discussion. Of course, if the house is agreeable to having it accepted, then I shall abide by that decision.

If I may speak to the point of order raised by the minister, I would say that if our subamendment involves a financial burden on the federal government, then the 

amendment also is out of order because it could be argued with equal force that the continuation of the equalization principle would involve a financial burden on the federal government. I feel, therefore, since the amendment has been accepted, the point of order in connection with the subamendment is hardly relevant.
May I point out that the amendment offered by the official opposition asks that the principle of equalization be continued in the federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements. All we are asking is that the equalization principle be continued and that, in addition, the principle be extended so as to provide sufficient federal assistance to the provinces in the matter of capital services.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the amendment speaks of maintaining a principle which has been recognized in the past. The subamendment suggests the extension to a specific field of earmarked funds. There are numerous citations to the effect that an amendment of this kind cannot further encumber the public revenues and I would suggest this subamendment is out of order upon the grounds stated by the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext: I should like to appeal your ruling, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext: Those in favour of sustaining the Chair's decision will please say yea.
Yea.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Those opposed will say nay.

In my opinion the yeas have it.

Mr. Speaker put the question as follows: The question is an appeal to the house from a decision of the Chair as follows: Mr. Cardin moved, in amendment to a motion to go into supply, as follows:
"That all the words after the word 'that' be struck out and the following substituted therefor: 'In view of the fact that the federal government at the October conference (1960) with the provinces proposed fixed subsidies in place of the equalization payments provided under the present tax-sharing arrangements, and that this October proposal is a repudiation of the principle of equalization;
Therefore be it resolved that this house strongly favours the continued application of the principle of equalization of direct tax revenues pledged to the provinces by the Prime Minister at the federal-provincial conference in July, 1960, and defined at that time by the Prime Minister as a payment by Canada to the provinces to bring the per capita return from the three taxes at standard rates up to the average per capita yield in the two provinces in which per capita yield is highest.' "That the amendment be amended by inserting after the word 'resolved' in the first line of paragraph 2, '(a)', and adding to the proposed amendment the following subparagraph:

speechtext: I declare the decision of the Chair confirmed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, whatever else may be said today concerning the pitch by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), it was certainly preceded by a long wind-up.
He undertook to touch on, I suppose, 15 or 20 subjects before he admitted the house to a view of the subject which he was proposing to raise on this supply motion. I suppose all hon. members shared the same impression as the speech proceeded. Probably all began with the assumption that this was another of the compositions of Professor Lamontagne-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order, a genuine point of order.
That is a change.
My point of order is that it is contrary to the rules of the house to reflect upon speeches made by hon. members or to suggest that they were written by someone else.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member spoke too soon, if this is the point on which he is so touchy, because I was going to say that before the speech had ended I think we had all concluded it was so bad that it must have been prepared by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill).

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps in view of the answer it is unnecessary to adjudicate.
I think so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is certainly something new, Mr. Speaker, to hear an hon. member, who was not present at a conference that proceeded in camera, rise and assure the house that what he is about to state is an accurate report of what happened at the conference, especially when that report comes from a well-known Liberal newspaper.
I think the accuracy of the hon. member's remarks throughout can well be tested by

the fact that when he did get down to something specific he found himself in the wrong column-I think he was in the wrong column all the way through his speech-and even then he did not get the right words.
Let me say in general terms concerning the speech of the hon. gentleman who introduced this motion that the speech was throughout based on wrong premises. It abounded in erroneous statements of fact. It was misleading in its purport, except in the quotation from the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
Which one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was the one
really accurate and reliable portion of his speech. Even if the speech has been accurate, even if it had been based on sound premises, it would have been completely out of date. It has led now to an amendment which is completely misdirected and which has no basis whatsoever.
I make only one comment on the form of the amendment. It is preceded by a preamble. We have not raised this question of order because we want to meet this amendment and invite the house to pass upon what is an invitation by the official opposition to express want of confidence in the government. Let there be no question about the purport of this amendment; it is a want of confidence motion, and therefore we wish to meet it, and meet it head on.
Just in case the point comes up on another occasion, I should like to say that I question whether on an amendment to a supply motion it is proper to introduce a preamble in the amendment.
But there is something more that is involved in the introduction of such an amendment at this time. This is an attempt to jump the gun. This is an attempt to cast into the midst of pending negotiations what is obviously expected to be a very serious obstacle and interference.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if you can conceive of a more irresponsible course for any opposition to follow than to attempt to introduce this matter into the realm of debate, while negotiations are still pending and while much of what has passed in negotiation has occurred behind closed doors, and when the opposition has not all the facts. While these negotiations are still proceeding, and when they know it has been proposed that the conference should resume, they now leap into debate and seek to muddy these waters and to follow a course which is calculated to make agreement between the federal and provincial governments more difficult.

I have no doubt whatever that hon. members opposite must have known when they introduced such an amendment at this time, at this particular stage of negotiations, that it would be construed by others outside this house as purporting to prejudice negotiations. We of the federal government are very hopeful of a good agreement being entered into between the federal and provincial governments in keeping with the policy that this government has followed from the moment it was sworn into office of doing justice to the provinces and their municipalities. Having regard to the national interest we shall continue to do in this fiscal field everything that is proper in seeking arrangements for the fiscal period commencing April 1, 1962 that will be fair to all levels of government.
How different was our course five years ago when we were in opposition. Knowing that these matters were proceeding in negotiation and that many of these negotiations were being carried on in camera, we did not seek to muddy the waters. We held the government responsible for the proposals which it brought into the house in the end, as was our duty. We held the government responsible and we attacked those proposals. We divided the house on the legislation by which the federal government of that day sought to place upon the statute books an enactment confirming the terms that the federal government had put forward. That, I think, is the proper course, not to seek to prejudice negotiations at this particular time.
We have heard something this afternoon by way of a review of history from the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres which, if it bears any resemblance to the fact and the record, does so, believe me, by pure coincidence. History has been rewritten this afternoon and any resemblance is most difficult to find.
I begin with 1957, with the change of government on June 21 of that year. We came into office and inherited an unholy mess left to us by our predecessors in relation to federal-provincial fiscal relations. Of all the lamentable failures of that previous government I suppose none was worse than in the realm of dominion-provincial fiscal relations, leaving aside for the moment the way in which hon. members opposite sought to destroy the effectiveness of parliament and its dignity.
Let me enlarge on what I have said in regard to the unholy mess they left behind. I suppose never in the history of this country has there been a time marked by greater friction in dominion-provincial relations than 90205-6-98J
Dominion-Provincial Relations was the period of the late days of the former administration, that now long since discredited and unlamented administration.
Agreements had been made by nine provinces pursuant to the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act enacted by parliament in 1956. Yes, nine provinces had made agreements. Had they done so with any degree of alacrity and enthusiasm? No, Mr. Speaker. The attitude of nearly all the provinces was that they had no alternative, that virtually a pistol had been put to their heads.
We do not need to turn to what Conservative premiers said, nor to what the Conservative opposition of those days in this house had to say. Let me just quote some things that were said by Liberal premiers of that time. These statements have been put on the record of the house before, but let me briefly remind the house of some of these observations.
Let us turn, first, to a statement made by Mr. Campbell, the then Liberal premier of Manitoba. This statement was made on July 23, 1956 in commenting on the course of discussion at the conference of that year and the previous year and the hard and fast, take it or leave it proposals put forward by the stiff-necked federal government of that day. Here are Mr. Campbell's words:
However, Manitoba was still disappointed that so little attention had been paid to the question of the actual financial requirements faced by the provincial governments in the next few years.
Would the minister tell us the source of that quotation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And again;
It is our recommendation that before any new pattern in federal-provincial relations is adopted a thorough reassessment of the relative responsibilities and revenue sources of the various governments in Canada should be undertaken.
Would the minister say where that was taken from?

The minister has said those words were uttered by Mr. Campbell. A great deal turns upon when they were uttered and in what circumstances. The minister is using them in argument. speechtext: The hon. member has dealt with a point he has raised himself with which I should like to deal later, but in the interval I trust he will not allow to remain on the record the statement that the minister has fabricated a statement. Mr. Speaker, if I did not
appear to withdraw handsomely enough, let me now withdraw that statement unreservedly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The other point is as to whether an hon. member using a quotation he has previously put on Hansard ought to have to verify its source. I think that verification is a matter or argument rather than of right. It seems to me an hon. member is entitled to quote what he said in Hansard at an earlier time if exception was not taken to it then. It is open to all hon. members to challenge the quotation if they have grounds for doing so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On the same occasion, Mr. Speaker, I also put on the record this quotation of Premier Matheson of Prince Edward Island, uttered at the same period:
No recognition of a province's fiscal need problem or its tax-raising ability was taken into consideration in the re-allocation or distribution of the tax moneys, but the same old factors were again used in the formula-the gross national product of Canada and the population of the provinces.
Here is what the provincial premier of Alberta had to say:
The federal government has retained for itself the broader and higher-yielding tax fields and, plagued with its financial problems at national level, has failed to recognize the financial needs of its provinces and their municipalities.
We hope that the shift toward centralization of governing authority which has resulted from a complex system of grants will be reversed so that more than ever the decisions can be made by representatives close to the people.
Those are not the words of Conservatives. Those are the words, in two cases, of Liberal provincial premiers and in the third case of a Social Credit provincial premier.
It was not a happy settlement that came into effect on April 1, 1957. It was a series of arrangements that the provinces disliked and denounced and which we, then the official opposition in this house when this legislation was presented by the government in the summer of 1956, attacked and voted against because we said it made inadequate provision for the provinces. That was the situation when we came into office. The agreements were already in existence. We have carried out those agreements to the letter, and we have added very substantially to the payments that have been made to the provinces, whether by way of conditional or unconditional grants, since that time.
In November, 1957 we called the first of what has now become a formidable series of dominion-provincial conferences in the past

three and a half years. One striking fact stood out in that conference. That was that the federal government, this new federal government, was taking an entirely new attitude toward the provinces in such meetings. Gone was the old stiff-necked attitude of the former administration, that take it or leave it attitude which had stood out in their dealings and was demonstrated at the previous conferences. The attitude shown by the new federal government earned the warm-hearted praise of many of those attending the conference representing provinces, and by no means all from provinces with Conservative governments.
Then we come to the early days of 1958 when the federal government moved swiftly to enlarge, and to enlarge substantially, the benefits provided for the provinces. Two outstanding measures were introduced at that time. The first was to increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax. The second was the introduction for the first time in history of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants. Let me say very simply but very emphatically, Mr. Speaker, that had there not been a change of government there would have been no increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent to the provinces of their share of the yield from the personal income tax, and there never would have been an Atlantic provinces adjustment grant.
These new measures have been in effect now for almost three years. They will complete the third year on March 31 next. The increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent in the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax has been in those three years worth to the provinces $200 million in round figures. The provision by way of Atlantic adjustment grants was at the rate of $25 million a year for the four years commencing April 1, 1958. In those three years, then, those three fiscal years that have almost concluded, those grants have been worth $75 million to the four Atlantic provinces. They have been worth $7,500,000 to Prince Edward Island; they have been worth $22,500,000 to each of the other three provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland. So you see, Mr. Speaker, these additional provisions have been worth to the provinces in those three years, in round figures, about $275 million.
We did not pay these out of any overflowing treasury, Mr. Speaker.
That's for sure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We did not have any big surplus to pay them out of. In order to aid the provinces and the municipalities
Dominion-Provincial Relations of the country we were prepared to enlarge our deficit and go deeper into the red to help them.
I have said that none of this money would ever have been made available to the provinces had it not been for the change of government. I go farther and say that when we hear these mealy-mouthed assertions about equalization payments, this government has nothing to learn from its predecessors or from the tattered remnant of our predecessors who bedeck the benches opposite.
The fact is, as I have said before in this house on previous occasions, the principle of equalization, by which we mean the principle of assisting provinces in fiscal need, assisting them out of the federal treasury, has been carried farther by this government than was ever done before, much farther than the former government ever dreamed of doing. The Atlantic povinces adjustment grant represents the farthest extension in this country's history of the principle of equalization in terms of meeting fiscal need of provinces. These are simply the provisions that have been made by way of amendment of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act; but they do not comprehend at all the total of the provisions made by the federal government on behalf of the provinces.
The previous administration claims credit for the increases that were made and that became effective on April 1, 1957. Yes, the agreements that were entered into at that time did provide for certain increases. But who has found the money in budgets year by year to pay those increases, as well as those substantial increases that were introduced, that would never have been made available to the provinces but for the change of government? It is the present federal government; and when hon. members opposite talk about our deficits we say that those who want to be fair in their judgments of such questions ought to be frank enough and just enough to remember that much of our deficit was attributable to the substantial increases year by year in aid to the provinces out of the federal treasury.
This has been placed on record before, Mr. Speaker; I do not need to delay the house in regard to it. You will find it on page 2676 of Hansard of March 31, 1960. You will see there, Mr. Speaker, what has been the total of federal payments to the provinces. I will just segregate for one moment the conditional payments, for the scope and the extent of those additional payments have been greatly enlarged since we came into office, and because of the enlargement of those costsharing programs these have to be paid for. And the federal government has been more generous than any previous government had.

Dominion-Provincial Relations been in offering assistance to the provinces in measures of this kind which fall under provincial jurisdiction, in their establishment and maintenance, and to which the federal government has been permitted to contribute.
If you look at that record, Mr. Speaker, you will find that the federal contribution to the provinces by way of conditional payments in the fiscal year 1956-57 amounted to $111 million. In 1957-58 they rose to $144.8 million; in 1958-59 to $248.1 million; in 195960, according to the then preliminary estimates, $383.3 million and acording to the estimate for 1960-61, $389 million. Since we came into office our contributions to these conditional grants to the provinces have increased more than threefold.
I give now the totals of payments of all kinds, unconditional payments, conditional payments, as well as those payments for the benefit of provincial institutions, namely university grants and grants to municipalities, in the past five years. They are:
