You will see, Mr. Speaker, that since we came into office payments out of the federal treasury to the provincial treasuries, whether by way of conditional or unconditional payments or payments to provincial institutions including universities and municipalities, have, speaking in round figures, doubled. Yet these hon. gentlemen opposite have the temerity to come into the house and pretend, and what a hollow pretense it is, to be the champions of justice to the provinces. We have nothing to learn from hon. members opposite about doing justice to the provinces. We want none of the injustices that they did to the provinces and the way in which they went about their work of centralizing power at Ottawa while not being fair to the provinces in fiscal matters.
Therefore, on the record with respect to the present period covered by the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, the five-year period that runs to March 31, 1962, we say that since the present government came into office there has been a notable improvement. First, there has been a notable improvement in the spirit in which the federal government has met the provinces and understood the problems of the provinces in discharging their constitutional responsibilities. Second, there has been a substantial increase in the amounts provided out of the

federal treasury for the benefit of the provinces and their institutions. Third, the principle of assisting provinces that are in fiscal need has been carried farther than it was ever carried before or dreamt of by our predecessors.
What is the outlook for 1961-62? I would think that the additional 3 per cent in the provincial share of the yield from the personal income tax may be expected in the next fiscal year to amount to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $70 million in round figures. There will be again $25 million to the Atlantic provinces, and the payments out of the federal treasury to the provinces by way of federal contribution to cost-sharing programs will undoubtedly be substantially larger than in any previous year.
Quebec's adherence now to a program of hospital insurance means that the federal treasury in what remains of the present fiscal year will be paying out an additional $13.9 million on that account, and it is estimated that Quebec's adherence to the scheme of hospital insurance will involve additional payments out of the treasury in 1961-62 in excess of $70 million. When people speak of the fact that the estimates for the year 1961-62 show an increase of $222 million over those for 1960-61 let me point out that over $70 million of the increase is accounted for in that way alone.
I pass on to the subject of the preparations for the fiscal arrangements for the period that will begin on April 1, 1962. There have been some half dozen preparatory conferences. Never before has so much effort been expended by the federal and provincial governments in studying the common problems that they face and in laying the groundwork for such arrangements as may be entered into after April 1, 1962. We have had meetings of the continuing committee of officials. There were two conferences of the finance ministers and provincial treasurers and there have been two plenary conferences in 1960 of the Prime Minister and the premiers of all of the provincial governments.
All of these meetings have been helpful. All of these meetings have been carried on in a good spirit. There are, of course, differences. Naturally each government has certain responsibilities which it must discharge in respect of those whom it represents, but the spirit has been good and if hon. members opposite will stop playing politics with this problem-
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-if they will stop trying to stir up trouble for their mean political purposes then I think we will go along very well in these dominion-provincial

plenary conferences and I think we can look toward something very much better than the provinces ever would have received if there had not been a change of government in 1957.
It sounded strange in the mouth of the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres this afternoon to hear him talk about the desire for more regular consultation. What an assertion coming out of the mouth of a member of the opposition, asking for more regular consultation. There has been more consultation already in connection with these proposed arrangements for the fiscal period beginning April 1, 1962 than there was five years ago in connection with those that came into effect in 1957.
What have we heard when we have reported to parliament on these further consultations? We have heard from the opposition only derision when we have talked about meetings of the ministers of finance and provincial treasurers, useful meetings that they were; when we have talked about meetings of the continuing committee of officials, a committee, incidentally, that was not set up by us but was set up by Mr. St. Laurent. This is another action of Mr. St. Laurent that has apparently been repudiated by his successors opposite who have forgotten the very great debt that they owe to Mr. St. Laurent. They would never have sat on the treasury benches had it not been for Mr. St. Laurent and I think it was very shabby treatment that they accorded to Mr. St. Laurent in 1957 and 1958. It is no credit to them now to try to repudiate what Mr. St. Laurent did in setting up this continuing committee of officials.
Let me say a further word now on the subject of the two plenary conferences in 1960, the one held in July and the other in October. These, as I have indicated, were carefully planned conferences. The meeting in July was called principally for the purpose of giving the provinces full opportunity to state their views, their claims, yes, their demands. Of course they readily responded and they did state their demands. As was my duty I had to make some reckoning of what these demands aggregated and I gave the house the figures. I do not need to delay the house now, Mr. Speaker, with those figures, but I can remind the house of the fact that the demands of the provinces were marked by extraordinary diversity.
It would not have been too easy to harmonize all the demands of the provinces. Apart from the problem of conflict in the nature of the demands, there was the problem of cost. If you look back at Hansard for August 10, 1960, page 7930, you will find that
Dominion-Provincial Relations I put on the record just some of the demands that were made upon us. I estimated these demands as there categorized would have cost the federal treasury between $2,080 million and $2,055 million per annum. This was not an exhaustive list.
It is worth recalling what the Winnipeg Free Press had to say at that time on this subject. Here, I expect the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to sit up and take notice because I refer to the Winnipeg Free Press, from which he has never been known yet to derogate. This is an editorial that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of August 16, 1960, and I quote:
There is no reason why the provinces' demands should not be met-if the people of the provinces are prepared to pay for them. They cannot, however, expect the federal government to hand out an extra $2 billions every year without getting the money from somewhere. The present federal budget is just under $6 billions. Of this, about $1.5 billions goes for defence, another $1.5 billions to the department of health and welfare-largely for children's allowances and old age and other pensions.
The federal government could, therefore, almost meet the provincial demands by eliminating entirely our spending on defence or by doing away with family allowances and all pensions. Clearly that is impossible.
I interject there and say that it is impossible unless the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is going to propose it.
Equally unattainable is the hope of reducing other government expenditures to anywhere near the point that would free enough money to meet the provinces' requests. The only alternative (outside of printing more money and shoving the country over the edge of the financial precipice) is for Ottawa to raise the extra $2 billions by raising taxes to produce this sum.
To grant the provincial demands would mean an increase of about 40 per cent in the federal budget. That is the amount of increase we could then expect in all the taxes we pay-income, sales, excise and so on. Faced with a tax increase of this proportion, however, it may be that the vast majority of the taxpayers will join with Mr. Fleming in crying "halt" to the premiers' demands,
I am sure that statement will not be attacked by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
This afternoon we have heard some curious misinterpretations of the position taken by the Prime Minister at that July conference. If ever a statement was plain, plain for all to read, plain for all to understand, it was the statement made by the Prime Minister at the opening of the conference on July 25. It seems that hon. members opposite are not content to have a plain statement. Instead of interpreting it in accordance with its plain terms we have heard a most interesting but most inaccurate gloss put upon the words of the Prime Minister this afternoon.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Here are the words of the Prime Minister. Can you imagine anything clearer, more straightforward or more emphatic than these words? What the Prime Minister stated on July 25 is the position of the federal government today and will continue to be the position of the federal government. I quote:
Some provinces have indicated a desire to resume the collection of their own revenue from these tax fields.
He was speaking of the standard taxes, the personal income tax, the corporation tax and the succession duty or estate taxes. He continued:
This raises a question which will have to be considered in the course of this conference hut I want to make this abundantly clear on behalf of the dominion government that whatever the ultimate decision may be the principle of equalization must be preserved.
We had to sit here this afternoon and listen to the hon. member opposite talk as though that statement had never been made.
He quoted it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then he proceeded to misinterpret it in a way that would do justice to only the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I continue the quotation from the Prime Minister's statement:
Equalization, the second component, is a payment by Canada to the provinces to bring the per capita return from the three taxes at standard rates up to the average per capita yield in the two provinces in which per capita yield is highest. For provinces in which the tax potential is relatively low, this principle is the most important.
It might be noted in passing that earlier arrangements did not recognize the principle of equalization explicitly although it was to some extent implicit in the "per capita" basis of payment.
Again I wish to emphasize that the federal government remains firmly committed to the principle of equalization and of financial assistance to those provinces in which incomes and taxable capacity are below those of the richer provinces. Indeed,-I think this is worthy of being pointed out-through the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, this government has carried this principle further than ever before. Last year the total payments for equalization and other fiscal aid grants amounted to $215 million as compared to $138 million in 1957-58, which was the first fiscal year in which the present act has been in effect.
The government believes that the principle of fiscal aid and equalization to assist the less wealthy provinces stands on its own feet and is accepted on that basis, and is quite separate from the question of tax rental or tax sharing.
I doubt, if any clearer statement has ever been made at a dominion-provincial conference. I do not know how it would be possible for anyone to make a clearer statement than the Prime Minister made on that occasion. That was the position of the government on July 25, 1960, and that is the position of this government on this 30th day of January, 1961. It is the position this

federal government will carry into the further conferences and exchanges that remain to be carried out before the new arrangements are finally consummated.
I come now to the October conference. I have indicated that at the July conference the floor was largely occupied by the provinces in stating their demands. At the October conference, the Prime Minister on behalf of the federal government put forward, not any take it or leave it proposition, no package proposal, but what were described by him and treated throughout the conference as suggestions. This was made very clear at the outset by the Prime Minister. No delegate attending the conference in any capacity was under any misunderstanding of the status of these suggestions. They remained suggestions throughout, and indeed the flexibility of the federal attitude as demonstrated by the Prime Minister in that conference won praise.
So, Mr. Speaker, let us be quite clear about this. When the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres this afternoon talked, as he did, about the Prime Minister assuming an arrogant attitude, an attitude that was downright insulting to the provinces, he was talking about something about which he knew nothing. He was making a statement that flew right in the teeth of the fact and of the truth. I hope I have made myself plain, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres rises in this House of Commons today and makes these baseless, irresponsible statements, but no such statements were made by any of the provincial premiers at that conference. Not one of them had anything to say by way of disagreeing with or condemning the attitude taken by the Prime Minister.
Page Mr. Bennett.

What about some of the provinces closer to home, if the peregrinating hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has any place that he calls home now in the various provinces? Wherever home may be, let us hope that in his case it will be "Home Sweet Home". However, evidently

speechtext: I do not think I will do so now, Mr. Speaker. Let me make it clear that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate does not know first hand what happened in that conference. If he is upholding what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres in attributing to the Prime Minister an attitude that was arrogant or insulting to the provinces I must say to him that he has been misinformed. He is proceeding from a source of information that is not accurate or reliable.
I only read the newspapers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then my statement stands, namely that if there is any newspaper or any person that says that the Prime Minister took an attitude at that conference that was arrogant or insulting to the provinces, it or he is resorting to a source that is untrue and unreliable. Let us not have any more nonsense about that matter by hon. members opposite.
The Prime Minister was thanked at the conclusion of that conference by those who were there for the way in which he had conducted the conference. He was thanked for his flexible approach. This was the way in which the provincial premiers reacted to the attitude of the Prime Minister. They did not act in the way in which the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres says, based on his lack of knowledge of what occurred there and supported by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate proceeding on his enormous lack of knowledge of what happened at the conference. So much for the attitude.
The federal government through the mouth of the Prime Minister laid before that conference certain suggestions that were discussed freely and at the close of the conference it was indicated that the views put forward by the provinces would be studied and considered. That promise, like all the promises of the government, has been fulfilled to the letter. The views of the provinces have been most carefully reviewed and studied. We have considered those views in the light of their earlier demands, in the light of the federal fiscal position and indeed in the light of all relevant circumstances.
I pointed out that the suggestions put forward by the Prime Minister at that time took account of the demands that had been made in certain provincial quarters for release from what was described in those quarters as a strait-jacket.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
In all of this we sought to have due regard and due respect, which we think any federal government owes, for the sovereignty and autonomy of the provinces as well as for the responsibilities which they carry under the constitution. There was no such thing contemplated as, to use the expression that has fallen from the mouths of some hon. members opposite, a return to the tax jungle. As a matter of fact we said that if in the end a decision were reached that all or any of the provinces were to assume responsibility for levying and collecting taxes, the federal government was prepared to undertake the collection. Hence there will be no question at all about multiplicity of forms or return to a tax jungle. A tax jungle is the sort of thing that I think has existed in the minds of certain hon. members opposite. It certainly is not part of the thinking of the present federal government.
I have indicated the suggestions made by the Prime Minister of what would be involved. There were reasons why the provinces should at that stage have been offered their freedom to make their choice because, as some provinces reminded us, when the tax agreements were first introduced the provinces opposed them. The situation has changed to the extent that some provinces now want the federal government to go on levying and collecting their taxes. At that time I had occasion to point out how far this situation has gone in Canada. It has gone to the point where the provinces in the aggregate are drawing practically one third of their revenues out of the federal treasury.
This point was discussed, namely whether in a country operating under the kind of constitutional system we have that is a sound situation. But, as I indicated a while ago, even if the baseless assertions that have been made by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres this afternoon had been true or had been based on fact, they would still be completely out of date. The hon. member completely overlooked the status of the suggestions put forward by the Prime Minister at the October conference. They were not proposals. There was no package put forward as was the case with the St. Laurent government five years ago. These were merely suggestions for which the federal government took what was recognized by the provincial premiers in that conference as a flexible attitude and approach. Then the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate had this to say. Here is bravery for you. Here is a Canadian Press dispatch from Ottawa, January 11.
What year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The year is 1961, the year in which the hon. member for Bon-avista-Twillingate was supposed to grow up but did not do so. It reads in part as follows:
J. W. Pickersgill said today the Conservative government is trying to destroy the federal-provincial tax-sharing system which he described as one of the greatest acts of statesmanship of the former Liberal government.
"We Liberals are not going to let them do it," Mr. Pickersgill told the national Liberal rally.
In the face of these thundering words we have just been shaking in our shoes ever since. This is enough to strike terror into the heart of anyone who hears these thundering declarations by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate. His assertion has no truth in it; it flies in the teeth of fact. When he says that the present federal government is trying to destroy the federal-provincial tax-sharing system he is being truthful only if he puts a completely distorted interpretation on what he means by the federal-provincial tax-sharing system.
Hon. members opposite know this perfectly well. As I said earlier this afternoon, they are trying to jump the gun; they are trying to make speeches to redeem these thundering threats by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, because he knew perfectly well the status of the suggestions, that these matters were going to be further discussed, and that exchanges were in the course of being prepared. So just to satisfy his ego he puts up the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres
[Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) .1
this afternoon to make the speech that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate should have made, if he is prepared to assume paternity for what was uttered here this afternoon, so that his threat as reported in the Canadian Press dispatch that I read might not look to be completely repudiated by his own party. So he jumped the gun and had this speech made this afternoon.
Let me do now what should have been done tomorrow or the next day in the house. The Prime Minister this afternoon stated at the opening of the house that a letter had gone to all provincial premiers proposing a resumption of the conference. That letter, of course, is in the mails and normally it would not be read in the house until received by the provincial premiers. But I think the provincial premiers will understand why it is proper at this moment to read this particular letter, in view of the fact that hon. members opposite in their speeches and in their amendment are seeking to cast the federal government in an entirely false light. It is for that reason, and having regard to the fundamental fairnesses that are involved in the situation, that I should like to read the letter that has gone to all the provincial premiers. It has been signed by the Prime Minister and it reads:
The dominion-provincial plenary conference called to discuss fiscal arrangements for the period following March 31st, 1962, adjourned on October 28th last to meet at the call of the Chair. Is seems appropriate now that steps be taken to reconvene the conference. I propose that the meeting be resumed in Ottawa on February 23rd and 24th.
I am sure that all governments have been studying this important subject further with a view to arriving at a satisfactory and workable understanding. The suggestions which I have placed before the October conference included the principles of equalization based on fiscal need and the stabilization of provincial revenues. The federal government is also prepared to make provision for a growth factor in the equalization formula. It is our hope that agreement may be arrived at on the basis of these principles.
I realize that on account of the sitting of parliament and the legislatures this is a very busy time for us all. I hope, however, that you may find it possible to be present at the reconvened conference on Thursday, February 23rd, commencing at 10.00 a.m. If these dates are not regarded by the majority of the provinces as convenient, I would suggest alternatively March 23rd and 24th.
So the attempt of the opposition this afternoon to cast the government in a false light fails. There is the answer, the vindication of the principle of equalization, the vindication of the principle of stabilization and the acceptance of the concept of the growth factor as attached to the principle of equalization. So everything that has been said by the opposition this afternoon is proved now to have been an utter and hollow sham. The government will proceed with its planned program. It will meet the provinces in conference. It

will discuss their further proposals and submissions, and in the same attitude as has characterized the approach of the federal government previously we will, as the Prime Minister assured the provinces at the October conference-as he had earlier-seek in the true Canadian spirit to arrive at workable and satisfactory accords and understandings.
As has already been indicated to the house, it is the wish of the government to conclude the discussions and conferences in time to present a measure to parliament at this present session to provide the legislative authority for such arrangements as may be entered into with respect to the period commencing April 1, 1962.
One thing I make abundantly clear, that we have at all times stipulated in these conferences

and I repeat it now-that the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants shall be continued and that they shall be continued as Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, not denied their identity, as seems to be the thinking of hon. members opposite. They want to make them merged, blurred and obliterated in some general formula. Well, we have said, and we repeat, that the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants deserve to continue to stand on their own feet, and we propose to continue them. Likewise we shall continue the provision of the $8 million per annum for the province of Newfoundland to assist that province to bring the level of its services up to those of the other provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I see it is six o'clock. I do not wish to retain the house beyond six o'clock. Will you call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the six o'clock adjournment I was making some reference to the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and was drawing attention to what seems to be a developing difference between the government and the opposition. I pointed out that there was a very great difference between us at the outset, for the former government made no attempt to introduce any Atlantic provinces adjustment grants or to recognize the special position of the Atlantic area in relation to the problem of fiscal need, and that had there been no change of government there would never have been any such thing as Atlantic provinces adjustment grants.
Let this further distinction be drawn very clearly. Throughout these negotiations the
Dominion-Provincial Relations federal government has maintained very firmly the principle that the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants must be continued. They must be continued as what they can claim to be-Atlantic provinces adjustment grants-a recognition on the part of parliament of the special position of the Atlantic area in relation to this principle of equalization.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres this afternoon made it quite clear-I take it he was speaking for his party; he was certainly speaking for the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and that probably is the party-that it has now become a policy of the Liberal party to blur out the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, simply to leave their problem to be taken care of in general terms by some general formula. The public will have its opportunity to decide which policy it wishes. There is a clear difference drawn here between the government and the opposition in this policy. Let there be no doubt. We will stand firm for the continuance of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants as a separate form of federal aid to this particular area.
I was surprised indeed that this position should have been taken by the Liberal opposition. Perhaps one should not be surprised. They have played politics of late to an increasing degree with everything upon which they have been able to lay their tongues. But at the dominion-provincial plenary conference in 1957 this statement emerged in the agreed communique issued at the conference:
It was generally agreed that the over-all economic position of the Atlantic provinces is now such as to justify some special grants in aid to the governments of those provinces from the federal government.
Note those words, Mr. Speaker:	"some
special grants in aid to the governments of those provinces." That is the position of the government; it maintains special grants in aid for the Atlantic areas.
That leads me to make this comment also in relation to the payments to Newfoundland. We made it equally clear at the conference that regardless of what else might be agreed upon eventually in relation to equalization, stabilization, tax-sharing or anything else, we stipulated the continuance (a) of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and (b) the payment of $8 million yearly to the province of Newfoundland. We now have the Liberal party setting up a new policy here, that all of this is to be blurred and submerged. It will be interesting to know what the premier of Newfoundland will have to say about this suggestion that the special provision of $8 million for Newfoundland to enable that province

Dominion-Provincial Relations to help bring the level of its services up to those of the other Atlantic provinces be now blurred and submerged. It will be interesting to hear what he will say when he learns that his political kith and kin in the house are now saying in effect, "Oh well, merge these, submerge them, blur them and just get some general formula of general application."
That is not our position. We say that these are distinct grants and they will continue as distinct grants in the policy of the present government.
I have been conjuring as best I could the reason that has prompted the official opposition to follow the course it did this afternoon. On all previous occasions it was the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who selected himself as the opposition spokesman on dominion-provincial relations. I do not recall any case in which the hon. member has permitted anyone else to share this distinction with him, although I believe last year he permitted the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) to take some part in the debate in relation to the problem of university grants. Always, however, the spokesman on this subject has been the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. Today for some reason or other the hon. member sits back, for the time being at any rate, and it is the distinguished and popular hon. member for Riche-lieu-Vercheres who is permitted to make the speech.
This is an interesting departure from the established tactics. I think we can draw only one conclusion from this departure. It is that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate realized that the course being taken this afternoon by the opposition was so utterly irresponsible that he did not want to have his name tagged on to the amendment. It was generous indeed of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to be willing on this occasion to share with the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres the distinction of being spokesman for the official opposition on matters pertaining to federal-provincial fiscal relations. I suspect, however, that there was an Ethiopian in the woodpile someplace.
It was a striking fact this afternoon that after all the interest displayed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), and I think one or two others, last Friday, on the subject of the calling of a dominion-provincial conference and the exchange of communications with the provinces, when the Prime Minister on motions this afternoon introduced his statement which one would have thought under any circumstances would be regarded as a very important one, the kind of statement that would have been followed at once, seeing that it was made on 
motions, by a statement from the official opposition and then a statement from the C.C.F. and no doubt questions on the orders of the day, probing for more and more information, there was silence. Did it not strike you as odd today, Mr. Speaker, that silence followed the statement by the Prime Minister. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had no statement to make. He was the senior member of the official opposition in the house. Their ranks were badly depleted.
But some of us were still here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This golden opportunity to make some comment he allowed to go by default, a most extraordinary circumstance, Mr. Speaker.
Very suspicious.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There was ample time on the orders of the day. Today the period was rather shorter. From the whole of the official opposition there was not one question on this subject. I think the reason is plain. It is quite plain that the official opposition did not want any more information on this subject before they introduced their amendment and made their speeches. The less information that came out today in regard to the federal government's position the better from their point of view because they wanted to argue as though they were facts which were not facts, and so they wanted no information. They wanted to bring out nothing further in the way of fact or information for the house. They wanted to go ahead and argue this in the hope that no further information would come before the house before they argued their sorry case.
I think this is about as sorry and irresponsible an exhibition on the part of the official opposition as we have seen or, I hope are likely to see for a very long time. Whatever may be said about their demeanour and their performance when the Leader of the Opposition is present, all I have to say is, if this is the best they can do when he is absent, they had better get him back soon or get a message off to Essex East.
I am interested as well in the fact that when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate for a moment allowed his mantle to be worn by one of his colleagues it was a member from the province of Quebec who was permitted to wear it on this occasion. I am left to wonder whether this is by way of giving notice to parliament that there has been a change of position in regard to this matter on the part of Quebec. Does this mean that the province of Quebec now espouses the case for tax rentals and wishes to rent these standard tax fields to the federal government?
May I answer the minister immediately. I was elected to the federal parliament and what I say here has to do with the federal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, not having had any answer to my question I continue to ask it.
Perhaps the minister should ask Mr. Lesage if he wants an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is perhaps not amiss for us in this house, when we see the curious tactics adopted by the official opposition today, to wonder whether this is notice, as I have suggested, that the province of Quebec, or the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres now thinks that the province of Quebec should rent these standard tax fields to the federal government?
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, not even the Minister of Finance, with all his words, can make me say things that I did not say. I never said any such thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not say the hon. member said that. I am drawing attention to the fact that with the zeal that the hon. member has demonstrated this afternoon he has assumed the role of spokesman for the official opposition-
The Liberal party.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -on dominion-provincial questions in what was intended, I am sure, by the opposition to be a very important statement and has apparently come out quite strongly on this matter. It is a fair question, I think, on the part of those who followed his statement with great care, to ask if this means that the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres has now become a convert to the theory of tax rental, and if he shares with the hon. member for Bon-avista-Twillingate this great enthusiasm for the tax rental system to the point where he thinks that the province of Quebec should change its position and now rent, or propose to rent, these fields of taxation to the federal government if the federal government were prepared to rent them?

I think I can answer that question, and I think the minister should let me answer it. I, as a member of the federal Liberal party, have always been in favour of tax rentals, and I have said so in the past. Regardless of whether the province of Quebec decides to go for tax rentals, my position has never changed since I have sat in this house.
Dominion-Provincial Relations

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member has made it quite clear that he supports a system of tax rentals.
That is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He has not dealt with the point I have raised. Does he advocate rental by the province of Quebec to the federal government of all these three fields of taxation?
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Gloucester rises on a point of order.
I wish to raise a point of order. Since when has a minister of the crown been allowed to ask a series of questions of members of the opposition in this house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
It is a point of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It seems to be natural in the normal course of debate to ask questions to which one does not expect an answer. I do not know of any rule of the house which compels or prevents another hon. member to answer if the member who asked the questions permits it. I think there is no point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I certainly can no longer expect an answer from the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres-
I would be willing to give one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -because he has said that he is an advocate of the system of tax rentals. He still leaves us wondering whether he advocates that the province of Quebec should rent these tax fields to the federal government.
That is the province's problem, not mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then, we are just where we were. The hon. member still has not answered the question and I suppose we will not even have an answer. We are left then in the position that the official spokesman of the Liberal opposition today on dominion-provincial relations has now proclaimed himself a zealot for the system of tax rentals, but when it comes to a simple question of applying those to the province that he knows best, apparently that is where the answers to the questions end.

Very, very feeble.

Dominion-Provincial Relations

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In leaving this question, Mr. Speaker, I can only express the hope that some day courage will rise and that the house will be afforded the opportunity of knowing what is the position of the hon. gentleman in regard to this very simple question that I put to him.
Would the minister permit me to ask him a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With pleasure.
Would he tell us what he thinks of Mr. Frost's $100 million inasmuch as the minister comes from the province of Ontario? Let him give a courageous answer to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Mr. Frost has throughout been very straightforward in the demands he has made on behalf of the province of Ontario-
So has Mr. Lesage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and he has based his demands upon principles that he conceives to be of general application.
So has Mr. Lesage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have never
known Premier Frost to advocate one thing for Ontario and something different for the other provinces. I will say this of him, that always what he has advocated has been applied to all provinces. I have not known him, when faced with a question as to whether he stood for something, to run away from the question of whether it did or did not apply to his own province.
I am asking where you stand, not where Mr. Frost stands.
I think the minister had better drop the argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May I draw attention now to the terms of the amendment. Earlier, I ventured to express a question with respect to whether it is proper in an amendment to a supply motion to introduce a preamble, but here is a preamble and perhaps I might say a word about it as well as on the operative part of the amendment. The preamble reads as follows:
In view of the fact that the federal government at the October conference (1960) with the provinces proposed fixed subsidies in place of the equalization payments provided under the present tax-sharing arrangements, and that this October proposal is a repudiation of the principle of equalization.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, the fifth word in this amendment. It says, "In view of the 'fact' that". I say that is not a fact. It is an untruth, and this amendment would be much more accurate if it read, "In view of the


untruth that the federal government at the October conference with the provinces proposed fixed subsidies".
It is quite true, that in the course of the group of suggestions that the Prime Minister put forward he made it quite clear that the principle of stabilization was being introduced into the suggestion with respect to equalization so that there would be no such thing as any drop in the amount of equalization that would be guaranteed to the provinces. He also invited the provinces to discuss among themselves how the sum should be distributed among them. In other words, he invited proposals from them. But, to call that a proposal in the sense in which the opposition uses the word "proposal" is, I say, to make this preamble a denial of the fact.
The operative part of the amendment reads as follows:
Therefore be It resolved that this house strongly favours the continued application of the principle of equalization of direct tax revenues pledged to the provinces by the Prime Minister at the federal-provincial conference in July, 1960

And so on.
Read the rest of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Very well. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate apparently has not read the rest of it so he asks me to do so. I continue:
-and defined at that time by the Prime Minister as a payment by Canada to the provinces to bring the per capita return from the three taxes at standard rates up to the average per capita yield in the two provinces in which per capita yield is highest.
Are you against that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That latter part is not a precise statement of the-
It is word for word.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not a precise statement of the position in regard to the principle of equalization. The Prime Minister made that firm statement that I quoted this afternoon in regard to equalization. The distribution is, of course, a matter to be agreed upon. As I pointed out at the conference, the principle of equalization is there. The principle of stabilization is there. It is fully recognized, it is fully supported. We have carried the principle of equalization farther than it has ever been carried before. The hon. member has gone beyond and has attempted to say in effect that equalization means just the same thing as it meant in 1957.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what he is asking the house to swallow tonight. So far as the principle of equalization is concerned, the sound principle of using federal revenues to meet the fiscal needs of certain provinces, nothing could be clearer than the statement by the Prime Minister, and I challenge anybody in this house to put in clearer words than did the Prime Minister on July 25 last the firm position taken by the federal government in relation to the principle of equalization, namely the principle of meeting fiscal need in the provinces.
It cannot be done. That is why we used those words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Pardon?
I said it cannot be done and that is why we used the Prime Minister's precise words as found on page 10 of this document.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member says it cannot be done. I do not know what the "it" is he is speaking of.

I will explain it to the minister. The minister said that the definition of equalization could not be described more precisely than it was by the Prime Minister. That was our opinion and that is why we used the Prime Minister's precise words taken word for word from the third paragraph on page 10 of the proceedings of the conference, and the minister is now repudiating them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, all that fury deserved a better cause and a stronger foundation.
Read the words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I read the words this afternoon. The hon. member is seeking to link two passages and put his own interpretation on them.
No, there is no interpretation by me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let me make it clear what the Prime Minister said. Here are his words:
-I want to make this abundantly clear on behalf of the dominion government that whatever the ultimate decision may be the principle of equalization must be preserved.
The principle of equalization.
Read the next two sentences.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The next two sentences go on to talk about how equalization is applied.
Equalization, the second component, is a payment by Canada to the provinces to bring the per capita return from the three taxes at standard
Dominion-Provincial Relations rates up to the average per capita yield in the two provinces in which per capita yield is highest. For provinces in which the tax potential is relatively low, this principle is the most important.
Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman is saying that the principle of equalization must always have attached to it the particular application or particular formula that he or his government attached to it in 1956, then I say that is an accretion on the principle of equalization. That is not the principle of equalization. At the conference we had different provinces suggesting changes in the formula, both the formula by which the amount is determined and the formula by which the principle of equalization is distributed among the provinces. No province that I am aware of treats the present formula as the principle of equalization. The principle of equalization is that out of federal revenues provision should be made with a view to helping those provinces that have fiscal need. That is the principle of equalization.
It is not what the Prime Minister said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is what the Prime Minister said. The Prime Minister, having stated the adherence of this government to the principle of equalization, pointed out the application of it in the present five-year period and under the present agreements, but no province has said that this is like the laws of the Medes and Persians, that this is immutable. As a matter of fact, I think a number of them, indeed I think the majority of them, asked for changes in formula.
In the rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, and they asked for changes in the formula for distribution too. You see, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was not at the conference. He always talks as though he knew everything but the fact is he does not know what went on there and he is just guessing now. It is simply guesswork in which he is indulging now. He is attempting to put glosses on the statements that no provincial premier would ever attempt to put on.
The provinces do not hold the former Liberal government in the same esteem in which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate holds it. They do not wish to have things continued as they were in 1956 under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act. They are hoping for something better. They know they have had something better since the changes were made in that legislation at the instance of the present federal government in 1958 and since.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate, then, has written what I would say

Dominion-Provincial Relations is a trumped up amendment. He knows, and no member of the house knows better than he that the government and every member supporting the government is committed to the principle of equalization, the principle of assisting provinces in fiscal need. At the same time he has drawn up this amendment knowing perfectly well it is a want of confidence motion and no member can support this amendment unless he at the same time expresses want of confidence in the government. If anyone else had done this the hon. member would be up denouncing it as trickery. What he is trying to do, you see, is put upon those hon. members who will vote against this amendment the appearance of being opposed to the principle of equalization.
We have seen what has happened before when parties have gone out on the hustings, have turned up Hansard, and tried to draw inferences from votes and from the terms of amendments without telling the whole story. I wish to make this plain statement. If after the vote is taken on this amendment anybody goes out anywhere, at any time, and portrays the government or any member of this house supporting the government as opposed to the principle of equalization he will be doing plain violence to the truth. He knows perfectly well that this is a want of confidence motion. It was introduced as such; it has that as its object.
My final word is on something that is most important in relation to the problems faced at the dominion-provincial level in any field, whether it be political, fiscal or otherwise. It is for this reason I have laid such emphasis today upon the spirit in which the present government has approached this problem of federal-provincial fiscal relations. This spirit was reflected by the federal government at the conferences. This is the spirit in which we intend to continue to carry on our exchanges, our dealings, our negotiations with the provinces of this country. It is the true Canadian spirit. It was in that true Canadian spirit that the Prime Minister, again in this opening statement at the conference on July 25 last, used these words:
We are fully conscious of the fact that the fiscal policy of the federal government has a considerable effect on business in Canada and on the financial position of the provinces and municipalities, and I can assure you this, that in shaping its financial programs the federal government has considered the interests of other governments and of the Canadian economy as a whole.
This year we will be making greatly reduced claims upon the capital market. Our net new borrowings will be about $210 million as compared with about $900 million last year and nearly $1,300 million in the year before that. The result will be that in reducing the volume of federal government borrowing so sharply the problems of provincial and municipal governments and of private

industry are greatly eased in meeting their essential financial requirements in the domestic market.
Our policies are and will continue to be designed to ease pressures on the capital market at a time of business expansion and at the same time resisting inflation.
Our financial policies have helped to reduce the reliance of other governments and private business on foreign capital markets, and the beneficial results are to be seen in the decline in the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar.
Then, later on, he said:
-I hope there will emerge mutually acceptable arrangements or agreements which will govern our financial relations in 1962 and subsequent years. I look forward to a most free, frank and friendly exchange of views.
My colleagues and I are anxious, I repeat, to hear your suggestions and your representations realizing at the same time that this conference will not make the final determination.
While conditions are vastly different from those of the founding fathers their dream of a united Canada has become a reality as the spirit of national unity becomes stronger through the years.
The federal system must be preserved and maintained and without centralization. My hope is that this conference will be a forward step to better things and that in a spirit of friendship and mutual respect we will condition ourselves again to the high ideals of the founding fathers thereby keeping faith with their great concept of a united Canada. We in turn will do our part to share the maintenance of equality of opportunity to Canadians in all provinces.
Those were noble words, Mr. Speaker. They breathed a noble Canadian spirit, and that is the spirit which animates the government of Canada.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, we, in the government simply wish to serve the best interests of the whole of Canada, with regard to fiscal relations between the federal government and the provinces.
Our aim is to respect at all times the constitution of the country. We recognize that the provinces have rights and responsibilities of their own which we have respected and shall continue to respect faithfully.
The government is firmly intent on contributing to the national unity of our dear Canada.
(Text) :

I did not want to interrupt the minister's usually verbose and unfathomable speech, but I wonder if he would be kind enough to tell the house whether or not the letter he read this afternoon was sent to the provincial premiers today, and if so at what time. Could he at the same time inform us as to exactly what is meant by the "growth factor" to which he referred in quoting the letter to the premiers, the reference being that a growth factor would be provided for in the equalization formula?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The letters were dispatched by Her Majesty's mail to all provincial premiers today before the house

met. This was made quite clear by the Prime Minister in his statement at the opening today. If the hon. member is not acquainted with the meaning of the words "growth factor", then I am afraid he has not gone very far in his researches into federal-provincial fiscal relations. This is one aspect of the discussions that proceeded in camera with which it is quite evident the hon. member is not familiar. I am sure all of the provinces will know the meaning of the expression "growth factor" and will have no difficulty whatever in correctly interpreting the letter of the Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, I think I should begin by congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on his first wind-up until six o'clock, at which point he announced he was concluding his speech; then he got his second wind which has been almost entirely pure wind. The minister, however, attempted to misrepresent the amendment before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is one thing to say "misrepresented" and it is another thing to say "attempted to misrepresent".

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is sometimes said that an hon. member misrepresents something but to say that he attempts to misrepresent, it seems to me, is contrary to the rules.
I do not think it is a very successful attempt because,-
Withdraw.
-as a matter of fact the minister had to read from the proceedings of the federal-provincial conference.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I trust that the hon. member will modify the initial statement "attempted to misrepresent".
Withdraw.

For the sake of economy of time I will waste no further time and will withdraw the remark. Unlike the minister, I have limited time of which I have no doubt the minister intends to use as much as he can in his customary manner.
This amendment, as the minister was obliged to admit, in the second part from the words "defined at that time by the Prime Minister" is word for word taken from page 10 of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Diefenbaker) statement to the federal-provincial conference on July 25. It was put in those terms precisely because that seemed to us to be an absolutely accurate definition of the principle of equalization as it seemed to me it was understood by everyone who understood it.

Oh, oh.
Dominion-Provincial Relations

We on this side of the house did not think we could improve on the Prime Minister's words in this particular. What the house is being asked to do, is to endorse the precise definition of equalization given by the Prime Minister. The Minister of Finance suggested that there is some trickery. He said he would not use the word but he said I would have used it if the conditions had been reversed. He said there was some trickery about this amendment. I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, what there is about this amendment. This amendment would never have been moved at all if the Prime Minister had not made his second statement or his suggestions, as the minister now likes to call them, in October which were in contradiction to what the Prime Minister had said in July. It was because of that contradiction that the amendment was moved.
Oh, oh.

I will call some other witnesses than members of the Liberal party on this particular point and some that are quite close to hon. gentlemen opposite on this precise point before I have finished with what I have to say.
I have no doubt that the government was greatly disappointed by this amendment. From what went on today before the orders of the day were reached it was obvious that the government thought the amendment was going to be to advocate the renconvening of the federal-provincial conference. The Prime Minister, with one of those-I will not use the word "tricks"-political devices which are quite legitimate, thought he would forestall that amendment. As a matter of fact, the calling of the federal-provincial conference is surely far less important than is the question of whether the federal-provincial conference, when called, is going to be able to rely upon the plain language the Prime Minister used in July or is going to be offered some substitute for it.
I must say that the terms of the letter are very equivocal. The Minister of Finance says that equalization has something to do with fiscal need. It is true that equalization helps to meet a fiscal need. However, as the minister also pointed out, it does not by any means completely meet it. Otherwise there would be no need for special grants to the Atlantic provinces. The definition of equalization has never been fiscal need. The definition of equalization has been, as the Prime Minister put it, to bring the revenues from the three taxes in all the provinces up to the level of those of the highest two. That is the definition of equalization, and the only definition there has been.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Either the government is going to stick by what the Prime Minister promised or it is not. We felt that this house ought to affirm that they were going to stick by what the Prime Minister promised in July and what he took away, in the opinion of some observers I think would be hard to laugh off.
I have here from the Winnipeg Free Press, a paper that now seems very dear to the Minister of Finance, of October 29, an account of a statement made by Mr. Roblin, the premier of Manitoba, when he returned from the federal-provincial conference. I do not intend to read all of his account. I simply want to deal with what Mr. Roblin said was the real point at issue. Here is what he said:
The real point at issue between the federal government and Manitoba, Mr. Roblin said, is the equalization principle which aims at giving the poorer provinces parity of revenue with the richest. He spoke out strongly against the federal proposals to freeze equalization payments at last year's level for the full five years of the new tax agreement.
That is Mr. Roblin's statement when he went back to Winnipeg. That is what he understood by the proposal or the suggestion of October. Mr. Roblin is not a stupid man. In fact, he is an extremely intelligent man and I think he understands this subject thoroughly. It will be noted that Mr. Roblin's view of what was proposed or suggested, if the minister prefers his euphemism, in October was precisely the view we took in this amendment. The plain fact is that if you fix the payment, as was suggested in October by the Prime Minister, at $220 million, that amount is the amount paid last year and there would be no growth factor of any description and there certainly would be no equalization in that procedure unless the revenues of the country remained absolutely stable or possibly, as the minister suggested, fell. I cannot think that even this government is so convinced that we are going to have depression conditions for the whole of the next five years that they regard a freezing of last year's payments as an adequate kind of equalization.
The minister in his speech also made something about another point. I do not intend to spend much time on it because it really had nothing directly to do with the amendment but since the minister raised it, I think it ought to be dealt with. He said that the Liberal party was trying to blur out the distinction between the Atlantic province grants, and indeed he also mentioned the payment due to Newfoundland under the constitution, as to which the position of the Liberal party has always been perfectly clear and has never been changed in any way, namely that it is a matter of right which ought not to be mixed up with this other matter at

all but should have been treated quite separately as a matter of right. But I suggest that it is very hard, if you read the Prime Minister's own statement last October, to draw any other conclusion than that this is precisely what the government is trying to do, because here is his second suggestion. This is the operative part:
To meet the needs of the provinces with lower tax potential we would therefore ask parliament to provide equalization payments or their equivalent in a total amount of $220 million a year-[DOT]
When you read the next page you find that $220 million is the sum total of the equalization element of the present payments to the provinces, plus the Atlantic provinces grant, plus the payments that should be made under term 29. That is what it is, but it is all blurred together and it is described in this way:
To meet the needs of the provinces with lower tax potential we would therefore ask parliament to provide equalization payments or their equivalent in a total amount of $220 million a year-
I say that if that is not blurring the thing, I do not know what blurring is. I think it is a good thing that that blurring has now been -and I hope the government does not change its mind again over this-removed tonight by the Minister of Finance.
He said that when this government came into office in 1957 they found federal-provincial financial relations in an unholy mess. If they found them in an unholy mess, that suggests, surely, there was something wrong with the system itself, there was something improper about the system. Yet three years later the Prime Minister goes into the railway committee room here on July 25, 1960 and pledges himself to maintain that very principle of equalization which the Minister of Finance said was in an unholy mess in 1957. I do not know which way you are to have it-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
I do not wish to be interrupted and I intend to continue.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the hon. member has said that I said the principle of equalization was in an unholy mess-
I did not say any such thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What I said was that the previous government had left this whole matter of dominion-provincial fiscal relations in an unholy mess.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister rises on a point of order, but what he does is contradict. If he is not satisfied with the interpretation of what he said he may correct it at the end of the speech, unless the hon. member cedes the floor.

I do not cede the floor, and I do not wish to cede the floor, because we have had far too much of this business. I repeat what I said-and it will be found in Hansard that this is what I said in the first place, if the minister had troubled to listen- that the minister had said that we left the whole situation in an unholy mess.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not what you said; you said, "the principle of equalization".

That is exactly what I said; and I said that three years later the Prime Minister came and pledged himself to maintain this principle of equalization, which was the principle of the arrangement in 1957 which the hon. gentleman describes as an unholy mess.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Utter sophistry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A non sequitur.
The minister calls it sophistry. If you have to listen to two hours of sophistry it is pretty hard to deal with some other commodity when you are replying.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do not misquote me.
The plain fact is that the principle of equalization, as everyone knows or ought to know-though I sometimes wonder whether some of the members on the treasury benches understand the matter at all-
I do not think you do.

Everyone knows, or ought to know, why the principle of equalization and the present tax sharing legislation were substituted for the old tax rental system in 1957. They were substituted for it in order to make it possible for all provinces to participate. Up until that time the former government of the province of Quebec-and the same attitude is taken by the present government- was not willing to rent their tax fields, and they are still not willing to do so.
However, we took the view that it was unfair to penalize a province on that account. That is why this tax sharing and equalization proposal was made by the St. Laurent government in 1955. Actually it was made formally in 1956; it was put up to the provinces and discussed in the autumn of 1955 and a formal proposal was made publicly and clearly so people could understand it. They did not have to ask questions in 1956 about what the growth factor meant.
The result was that every province accepted it. It is true that they were not content with the amount of money they received. The Minister of Finance suggested that even with the harmony that, he claims, now prevails in this country they would not be content
Dominion-Provincial Relations with the money they are going to receive. It is perfectly obvious that none of them were at all content with what happened last October. Indeed, I have here, and I think perhaps the minister will give to this the same respect he expects me to show for everything that appears in the Winnipeg Free Press a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of October 29, 1960. This is an article written by a newspaper man who has on the whole, I think been pretty friendly to the present government. It is written by Mr. Richard Jackson The heading on this article is:
Conference nowhere on tax deal, Jobless.
This is how it reads:
The federal-provincial conference got nowhere on either a tax deal or unemployment.
Tax negotiations would continue by mail, Prime Minister Diefenbaker has reported, "in an effort to resolve our differences".
There would be another round of talks next year, and, added the Prime Minister with emphasis, there would "have to be agreement before time run out on us all with expiration of the current tax agreements in March of 1962".
Then he goes on-and I will not read this- to say that even more bleak had been the performance of the conference on unemployment. That was the considered judgment of a reputable journalist in a Tory newspaper about that conference in October.
I was astonished that the minister read one paragraph from the Prime Minister's speech in July, where he talked about the federal government making no demands on the capital market, or very slight demands, in the next 12 months. That was based on the hypothesis of his $12 million surplus and not on the unpleasant facts that he was beginning to realize in October about his $300 million or $400 million deficit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are quite mistaken.

If the minister thinks he can get any premier to agree that he has made it easier for them to borrow he had better read what Mr. Bennett, Mr. Frost and a few of the rest of them said the day after he brought down his budget. I have some of their remarks here, but it would not be relevant to this debate, much as I would like to remind the Minister of Finance of what Mr. Bennett had to say.
The minister also made a great deal of the immense increase that the federal government, the present government, had made in payments to the provinces under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, including therein the Atlantic provinces grants. I admit that those were very welcome additions, and I would not be so silly as to say they were not. I have never at any time, as the minister knows, done anything but praise

Dominion-Provincial Relations the present government for the Atlantic provinces grants. The minister will find nothing that I have ever said to the contrary at any time, because I do like to be accurate about these things.
But I would remind the house and the minister-who knows it very well but never says it-that the change from the old tax rental system to the tax-sharing arrangements act which came into effect on April 1, 1957 resulted in an additional $100 million going to the provinces in the first year of the taxsharing plan over what they had received in the last year under the old arrangement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member not agree that I referred to that fact this afternoon? I did not mention the amount but I referred to the fact.

It was the first time the minister has ever done that. The minister was careful not to refer to the amount. In the Tory literature that my hon. friends opposite send around the country they always take the last full Liberal year, 1956-57. They claim everything else has been done by the present government. I could bring down that literature and read it to the minister and I shall do so in another debate.
The plain fact is that as a result of the additions that Mr. Harris proposed to this house in relation to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act of 1956, which came into effect on April 1, 1957, the provinces in the four succeeding years have received well over $400 million more than they would have received if those changes had not been made, and that is compared with the $275 million additional that the minister pointed out had been received by the provinces under changes in the law made by the present government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And we paid every cent of it.
Out of the minister's own pocket no doubt. The minister says they paid every cent of it. I will tell the minister who paid. The taxpayers of Canada paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member criticized us for having deficits.

The minister also said, "Of course, it was easy for the Liberals to do it because they ran the country well and had a surplus but it was difficult for me because I was running the country so badly that I had a deficit." That is a very slight paraphrase of what the minister said in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A gross distortion.
And the minister dropped a few tears, of course.
The hon. member said that, not the minister.

The minister took a great deal of credit for all these meetings that had been held prior to the meeting that has now been called for February 23 or March 23. Of course, when that meeting takes place there will have been, I believe, exactly the same number of meetings as were held before the 1956 bill was introduced in this house in a previous parliament. Precisely the same number, I believe. The procedure that has been followed has also been very similar indeed.
Notwithstanding the unholy mess we are supposed to have made of it, so far as these conferences are concerned the pattern has been extraordinarily similar as though someone had been-and I suspect someone was- looking up the precedents and telling hon. gentlemen opposite what they should do next. Evidently Mr. Frost thought that because he said in the legislature the other day that it was about the time at which it was customary to receive a letter from Ottawa to say what they would get. They are going to get a letter but it is not going to tell them what they are going to get. It is simply going to tell them that there is a growth factor, undefined. Everyone knows what a growth factor is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres. That hon. gentleman does not know.

I say without the slightest fear of contradiction that the government does not know what the growth factor is they are going to propose, that they have not yet decided what particular formula they intend to propose. I am not privy to the secrets of the cabinet but I have had a certain amount of experience and I am perfectly sure that if the government knew what is was going to propose to the premiers and if hon. members opposite were not ashamed of it, we would know it too.
The only reason it is described as a growth factor in that letter is that hon. members opposite do not know what formula to propose. They have not made up their minds. They have not decided. They are probably still arguing about it. There would not have been any letter today nor would there have been a growth factor proposed at this time, or for another couple of months as the Minister of Finance indicated on Friday-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The minister did no such thing.
-if the minister had not the impression-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is utterly untrue.
It is my opinion, and it is a matter of opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is flying in the face of the facts.
The minister knows very well that no letter had been written on Friday and no decision had been made on Friday to send a letter today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How do you know?
The minister knows full well-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was a reckless statement.

-that no doubt having a shrewd suspicion that this attempt to shortchange the provinces that was made last October would be protested in this house at the first available opportunity, the government thought it would be a clever thing to do to get this letter out today. Oh, I think it was quite a clever thing but it would have been a lot more satisfying to the provinces and to the country if that letter had stated in precise terms what this government was prepared to do in the way that Mr. St. Laurent did when he wrote his letter in January, 1956.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Did the hon. member compose it for Mr. St. Laurent?

The minister took delight in referring to Mr. St. Laurent's attitude. The minister enjoys going back to the speeches made in 1955. He does not read all of them but he does read some of them and draws from them phrases which he uses again and again. He described the Liberal attitude as inflexible and stiff-necked.
The fact is, of course, that after the letter in January, 1956, was sent another conference was held and a very substantial modification was made in that scheme as a result of the representations made by the provinces at that conference, as the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming) will well recall. It is true that all of the modifications the provinces would like to have seen made were not made and I venture to suggest-and here I am echoing the Minister of Finance and for once agreeing with him-that if all the suggestions from all the provincial premiers at these conferences were carried out there would be nothing left in the federal treasury. However, that is not the point at all.

Did you tell Mr. Lesage that?
Dominion-Provincial Relations

Of course, Mr. Lesage's proposals were very moderate compared with those made by the premier of Ontario who has the notion, apparently, that Ontario has some kind of prior right to every dollar that is earned by anyone in Ontario, and that any federal taxation levied in that province is, as his favourite organ the Globe and Mail says so often, stolen by them and handed out to people in other provinces to use it extravagantly.
I do not think this view that has been expressed by the Globe and Mail and that is expressed more and more by Mr. Frost will commend itself much to the minister's friends in all the other provinces. It certainly does not commend itself to the leader of the minister's and Prime Minister's party in the province of Saskatchewan because Mr. Pederson, again according to the Winnipeg Free Press of October 29, 1960, made a statement in Regina which is of some interest. The headline reads:
Saskatchewan P.C. chief blasts Dief on tax plan.
The article reads:
Martin Pederson, Saskatchewan Progressive Conservative leader, Thursday condemned Prime Minister Diefenbaker's proposals on new tax collection methods-
There is more to the same effect.
The plain fact is, as Mr. Walter Harris pointed out in his budget speech in 1957 in words that were simple and eloquent, the taxes imposed on the people of Canada by this parliament are imposed upon Canadians, collected from Canadians and spent on Canadians. That is the whole basis of any taxsharing arrangement that we have in this country, without which there can be no unity in this country.
I wish I had unlimited time at my disposal because I should like to read what Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding had to say about this in 1907, although they did not at that time have some of the modern techniques and notions we now have.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding pointed out at that time that the proper basis of federal subsidies should be a real per capita basis and not the rather extraordinary scheme that there was in the British North America Act, and changes were made in that direction.
