The minister objected to something some of my political friends had said about a return to the tax jungle. I lived in the tax jungle and I lived in what was perhaps the worst tax jungle because it was the most honestly run province in Canada in the depression. I refer to the province of Manitoba.
When I was a lecturer at United College in the province of Manitoba we paid a federal income tax and we paid a provincial income

Dominion-Provincial Relations tax, and in addition, a single man paid a 2 per cent wage tax on every dollar he earned if his income was over $480 a year. Every married man paid that wage tax on every dollar he earned if his income was over $960 a year. That tax was imposed by Mr. Bracken. It was imposed by Mr. Bracken because, instead of repudiating the provincial debt, as was done in some other provinces under some Other kinds of governments, or instead of allowing the unemployed to suffer, those who were employed were taxed and taxed very heavily indeed in order to see that there was no undue suffering, no more suffering than was inevitable from unemployment at that time.
But notwithstanding the level of taxation that we had at that time in Manitoba, and notwithstanding the honest efforts made by the government at that time to deal with those problems, it just was not possible with the tax base in that province, any more than it is in at least seven of the provinces of Canada today, to finance on that tax base and have taxes anything like the level they are in Ontario or in British Columbia and to provide anything approaching equal services.
If we do mean that there is to be reasonable equality of opportunity in this country, if we do mean that Canadians are to have an equal chance wherever they live, it can only be done in one of two ways. One is by centralization, by providing all the functions from this parliament here in Ottawa, which we turned our backs on in the Liberal party in 1937 when the Rowell-Sirois commission was appointed-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You turned back again later.

-and the other is, by putting all the provinces in a position by the equalization of the main tax fields to perform those functions by themselves. I am very proud that I belong to a party and belonged to a government that, from the tax jungle of the 1930's, accomplished the equalization that we had accomplished by 1957, which Mr. St. Laurent indicated was not perfect but was better-and every premier agreed with that- than anything that had been suggested up until then. Every one of them agreed with that without exception. I am very proud that I was associated with that policy.
I was very pleased, genuinely pleased, when I went into the railway committee room that day in July, 1960, and heard the Prime Minister make the statement that is in our amendment. I was pleased because I thought, well, they have had some experience now and they have seen the light, they realize that this is a difficult problem and that, until something


really better can be found, this is the best solution and I am going to praise them for it. That is what I intended to do until October. But I could not praise what happened in October any more than Mr. Roblin could, or any more than Mr. Stanfield could, or any more than Mr. Shaw could, or even any more than Mr. Frost could. As I say, it was because of this performance in October that we are debating this motion tonight.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You have brought the same motion in year after year.

If the government is prepared to go right back and say that they really, honestly meant, without equivocation, without interpretation, to carry out the plain words that the Prime Minister used in July, there will certainly be no criticism of the conduct of the government from me. But substitutes, ersatz things like growth factors and other phrases, such as equalization means fiscal need undefined, substitutes of that sort; birds in the bush that has not yet been cleared away in spite of the three and one half years of prodigious bushing are a very poor substitute for the bird in the hand that the provincial governments of this country have had since 1957 and that evidently, when the chips are down, none of them wants to lose.

Mr. Speaker, I presume that other hon. members were as much surprised as I was to see this amendment brought forward today by the opposition. Indeed, it seems to most hon. members, I am sure, as it does to me, that this whole amendment is a matter of great sound and fury signifying nothing.
Nothing was more obvious when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) was speaking than that all he was doing was setting up a straw man to knock down. His proposition is that the government is not sincere in espousing the principle of equalization, when the facts are clear to everybody that the government has always espoused the principle of equalization. No matter how hard the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate tried he could not bring forward one shred of evidence to show that there was any question in anybody's mind about this.
What about Mr. Roblin?
One thing in particular that surprised me was his reference to how happy he was in July, 1958 when he went into the railway committee room-
It was in 1960.

-and heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) there take a firm stand for the principle of equalization

Dominion-Provincial Relations
without any equivocation. There has been equivocation since then. The debate this afternoon as far as the Liberal party is concerned was a matter of knocking down a straw man.
Again I was surprised to see this topic brought forward when it is remembered that in this particular field the record of the Liberal party is worse than it is in any other, and that is saying a lot. If there was one thing more than another which defeated the Liberal party in 1957, it was their record in the field of dominion-provincial relations. Many people would blame the very obvious reluctance on their part to pay a reasonable old age pension to the older citizens in Canada, or the way in which they trampled on parliament in the last days of their arrogant rule. But I believe more than anything else their record in the field of federal-provincial relations defeated the Liberal party in 1957.
In his speech the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate himself admitted that. "None of the provinces", he said, "was satisfied with the arrangements in 1957". Mr. Speaker, I would say that that was a masterpiece of understatement. Actually, what was their record in the year 1956 and before? The most common news items in the papers of those days were those of the provincial treasurers and premiers trekking to Ottawa to beg a few crumbs out of the great surpluses that the Liberal party were piling up in Ottawa to bolster their sagging treasuries. In every situation even though the treasurers of the provinces were very hard up, and their provinces going without much needed essential services, the Liberal government of that day refused and insulted the premiers and treasurers who came forward looking for funds.
This afternoon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) put on the record the comments of the premiers of Manitoba and Prince Edward Island, both Liberal premiers, in respect of the attitude of the Liberal administration of that day. Certainly in my own province of Nova Scotia there can be no question as to what the niggardly attitude of the previous administration meant to the people of the province. In 1956, and in the years before that, in Nova Scotia we had an educational system coming almost to the brink of collapse because the provincial treasury was too poor to provide decent salaries to the teachers and decent schools for children to be trained in, or proper educational facilities generally. We had a highway system growing at a snail's pace and far short of the traffic requirements. We saw social welfare slipping away behind. Indeed, in some of the Atlantic provinces we
wondered at that time whether some of our governments might not be heading for bankruptcy in an attempt to provide essential services because of lack of help of any responsible nature from the federal government.
When the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate was speaking today, again speaking under the handicap that he did not have a shred of evidence to support the proposition he was putting forward-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: That would hardly stop him.

I have noticed, Mr. Speaker, that the louder and longer the tirade of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate the weaker is his argument. Certainly if he proved anything this evening it was not that he really doubted that the government was questioning the principle or the application of the principle of equalization; no, it seemed that he was worried that there might be some possibility of a weakening in the process of centralization at Ottawa, which was the factor upon which the Liberals based their fundamental thinking and their entire philosophy as to federal-provincial relations. If everything could be gathered together at Ottawa and if Ottawa could be in complete control of the provincial treasuries and the financial systems of the provinces, that would suit the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. That was the attitude of the administration of which he was a member a few years ago.
I should like to put on the record a few of the facts in relation to the record of the government in the field of dominion-provincial relations. Certainly it is a record of which the Conservative party, our Prime Minister, and his government can be very proud. In contrast to the days prior to 1957 when the treasury of my province of Nova Scotia was in such dire need, immediately after the government was elected in 1957 it called together the provincial treasurers and increased the provincial share of the income tax by 30 per cent, a very substantial increase. In addition, as has been said, it also provided $100 million over a four-year period in special grants for the development of the Atlantic provinces. When the Minister of Finance was speaking this afternoon he pointed out that between 1956-57 and 1960-61 contributions from the federal government to the provinces more than doubled. They increased from $689.4 million in 1956-57 to $1,300.9 million in 1960-61.
Perhaps more striking are the figures for Nova Scotia, which very much needed the transfusion that the Department of Finance provided in 1957-58 and following years. In 1956-57 unconditional grants to Nova Scotia

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that every member of this house is rather surprised to learn from the hon. member who has just resumed his seat that conditions are so good in Nova Scotia today. This is quite contrary to statements made in a speech delivered before a group of Conservative women right here in Ottawa on Friday last by one of his colleagues, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris). This hon. member stated publicly that conditions in Nova Scotia are bad.
The hon. member also stated that there has been no denial of the principle of equalization by the present government, and that the hon. member who moved the amendment, as well as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), did not have any evidence to support their arguments. I know that the amendment introduced this afternoon by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) is one which affects the needs of all parts of Canada. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had not tried to misrepresent our amendment I think we would be justified in saying that he gave his own version of the amendment which is quite different from ours.
The Minister of Finance, in his long and elaborate speech, said the present government had inherited an unholy mess in the federal-provincial field. We know also that the present government inherited a series of surpluses which have been turned into the worst series of deficits in the history of Canada. We know also that the present government inherited an unemployment insurance fund of $900 million, and that four months from now that fund will be completely depleted as a result of lack of leadership and mismanagement by this government. We know also that the present government inherited about 150,000 unemployed in the month of June, 1957. Since then the number of unemployed in this country has been at least two times, and in certain months three times as high as it was in any month under the previous administration.
We all agree that in order to achieve a high level of prosperity for all Canadians it is essential that the financial resources of the nation be available to provide the national government as well as provincial and municipal
1564	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations governments with adequate revenues to support public services. The need for public services such as roads, schools and other services provided by provincial and municipal governments is increasing yearly and imposing additional demands on those governments. Our growing population in this modern world is demanding more and more assistance, more benefits and more protection against economic and social hazards.
In order to achieve national prosperity, which we also agree is essential to national unity, the Liberal party believes that the principle of equalization in federal-provincial tax arrangements must be upheld, and that Canadians from every part of the country must receive an equal share of the revenues derived from national economic activities. The position of the Conservative party, notwithstanding what was said this afternoon and earlier this evening by the Minister of Finance, is far from being clear and definite on matters of such vital importance as the welfare of our population in every section of the country from one coast to the other.
Reference has been made by the mover of the amendment now under discussion to the ambiguous and contradictory statements made by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), first on July 25 last and then in October, to the provincial premiers who were convened at the last dominion-provincial conference. They were told then, notwithstanding the denials of the Minister of Finance, that the federal government was prepared to recommend to parliament that the federal tax rates in the three shared tax fields be reduced at the time of the termination of the present tax rental agreement, that is March 31, 1962, by the amount of the present standard rates, that is 14-9-50. I should like to quote the words of the Prime Minister, to which the Minister of Finance objected this afternoon, and I am quoting from a summary of suggestions made by the Prime Minister of Canada to the dominion-provincial conference on October 26, 1960. This document was made public following the Prime Minister's statement to the conference and was given to the press, so it is a public document. I am sure that the Prime Minister cannot deny that these are his exact words as reported in the statement which under his own instructions was handed to the press following that conference. Here are the Prime Minister's words:
To meet the needs of the provinces with lower tax potential we would therefore ask parliament to provide equalization payments or their equivalent in a total amount of $220 million a year, which is approximately the scale of the payments this year.


He went further when he said this:
The amount so provided will take the place of the present equalization payments, the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, and the special grants to Newfoundland under section 2 of the Newfoundland Additional Grants Act.
He went further and said this:
Being mindful of the necessity of maintaining a reasonable level of public services in areas of low tax potential, we will ask parliament to provide this sum of money for equalization payments.
That is a total of $220 million a year. We were told this afternoon by the Minister of Finance that at no time were such proposals made by the Prime Minister. I have here, Mr. Speaker, the Concise Oxford dictionary. Under the word "suggest" I find this definition: Propose. I wonder whether there is so much difference between a proposal and a suggestion made by the Prime Minister.
You can take a suggestion back more easily.

Probably so. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Mac-Lellan) said we had no reason whatsoever to doubt the Prime Minister's sincerity in maintaining the equalization principles. As to this offer that was made by the Prime Minister at the October conference, what would it mean to the various provinces? How would it affect those provinces such as the Atlantic provinces where the economic progress has been retarded by factors beyond the control of those provinces, with the result that the standard of living has fallen behind that of the rest of the country.
The freezing of the present equalization tax rate and the replacement of the present equalization payment to certain provinces including, to use the words of the Prime Minister himself, the Atlantic provinces, adjustment grants and the special grants to Newfoundland to a fixed sum of $220 million per year, as suggested to the provincial premiers in October last, is contrary to the principle of the equalization scheme. This is why we of the Liberal party felt that it was our duty to bring to the attention of the country the statement made by the Prime Minister and to object to the statement and to insist that the principle of equalization be maintained. No wonder the conference ended in failure and no wonder the premiers departed unhappy and dissatisfied and no wonder, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have now changed their minds.
In fact, to limit to $220 million a year the equalization payments to those provinces where the revenue yields are not sufficient to meet the needs of the provincial finance,

and to freeze such payments for a period of five years following March 31, 1962, is nothing else but a deliberate violation of a principle which has been accepted and recognized as just, equitable and practicable for the performance of those functions of national interest that are especially assigned to the federal government under our constitution.
However, I must admit that I am not at all surprised to hear such a proposal coming from the present Prime Minister. It is true-and I repeat this statement-that it is contradictory to the declaration he made on July 25 last when he said that the principle of equalization must be preserved and when he added that the federal government remains firmly committed to that principle. The Prime Minister knows, as does every Canadian taxpayer, that every dollar of federal revenue comes from the pockets of the Canadian taxpayer and that every dollar contributed by the federal treasury in stabilization or equalization payments is contributed by Canadian taxpayers.
As Mr. Harris said in his budget speech of March 14, 1957, as reported at page 2218 of Hansard of that date:
Canadians living in Ontario pay exactly the same rates of tax as are applicable to all other Canadians, and Canadians living in Ontario derive their incomes in considerable part, directly or indirectly, from consumers and producers in other parts of Canada, just as Canadians elsewhere may derive part of their incomes from business activity that takes place in Ontario.
At no time should the federal government give thought to the idea of abandoning the objective of the tax rental agreements which make it possible for all provinces to perform their constitutional functions. The suggestion offered to the provinces by the Prime Minister in October last, namely the freezing of the equalization payments to $220 million, which was supported this afternoon by the Minister of Finance, was nothing else but an offer concealed by an artificial cloud or a smoke screen. It was strategy for a take it or leave it proposal.
If the present government was to remain in power for many years,-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And it will do so.
Oh, oh.

This government has
reached the point where we are back to the Bennett days, where soup lines are being introduced, where surplus food products are being offered to the unemployed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Although we are now discussing an amendment proposed by our friends opposite concerning federal-provincial relations, the hon. member is now embarking on a complete side issue. Under the circumstances I think the rules should be observed.

If I may be allowed to do so, I should like to speak to the point of order, Mr. Speaker. I am speaking of the national growth of this country. We know that the tax ratio is being based on the gross national income. We know that the gross national income has an effect on the taxes and on the grants that would be made to the provinces. If the gross national product remains at the present level it would mean that this government will be limited to making payments which were about the equal of what they have been in the last fiscal year.
So I feel that my remarks are absolutely related, just as much as the remarks made by the Minister of Finance, who went far afield and spoke of national defence and so forth. The Canadian public is aware that this government lacks the leadership that is required to maintain the growth which prevailed in the last decade, in most of the 1950's under a Liberal government and which has practically reached a stalemate in the last three years since the present government took office.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is just fantasy.

It is no wonder that the apparent failure of activity to increase at the
1566	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations pace to which business has become accustomed has raised many questions and is causing so much concern in our country at the present time.
As I said earlier, the suggestion of the Prime Minister could be acceptable to certain provinces if, and only if, his government were to remain in office for the next five years; but we all know that such will not be the case.
It will.

Look at the Gallup poll that came out last Saturday. I am sure it gave you reason to worry.
The decade of the 1960's, which has begun on a far less expansive note than marked the beginning of the 1950's will, under a new Liberal administration, and very soon, regain its momentum and mark once more a period of progress and prosperity, a period where the growth of the richer provinces will enable the federal government to help proportionately, and on an equal basis, the poorer ones. This is why most of the provinces, and the Atlantic provinces in particular, cannot accept the Prime Minister's suggestion that the provinces be frozen at the 1960 level-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question. Will he tell me what the Atlantic provinces are getting under this decadent and failing government compared to the powerful and prosperous government which was defeated on June 21, 1957.

Under the present government the Atlantic provinces are in a worse position today than they have been for years. In the Atlantic provinces the number of unemployed today is over 15 per cent of the labour force.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The hon. member needs to call a psychiatrist. I will not say the hon. member is falsifying, but he needs a psychiatrist.

If a psychiatrist be needed I think he could be used on many of the members opposite. That is the situation in the Atlantic provinces today, and I would refer the minister to the situation in Pictou, and everywhere in the Cape Breton area. I know the hon. members opposite cannot keep quiet, because it hurts them to hear these things.
Under the Liberal principle the provinces were protected in case of inflation, while under the proposal made by the Prime Minister in October last-a proposal which he has amended and changed today-the dollar value of the federal payment will shrink by the full amount of such inflation. Such a proposal, if accepted, could destroy the progress made

in the federal-provincial tax-sharing field following the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois commission of 1937, and the provinces will be compelled to return to the strangling position they were in during the early 1930's in the days of the Bennett regime.
For a sound economy it is important to retain the principle of equalization and also the related principle of stabilization. As I said earlier there is no decrease in the needs for roads, schools and other essential public services provided by provinces and municipalities. Under our constitution it is the responsibility of the federal government to protect the provinces against any serious decline in their revenues from the sharing of taxes.
Our provinces, and our municipalities in particular, are being called upon to undertake capital projects which come within their jurisdiction and responsibility as a fundamental part of our Canadian federation. It is only logical to presume that reasonable men willing and desirous of living in a federation might agree to consider their common fiscal and administrative woes and make every effort to provide a series of working ideas.
This is where lies, and must be retained, the principle of equalization. The need for additional revenues for our municipalities is an urgent one and no one can deny that in order to discharge their constitutional responsibilities our municipalities must have adequate sources of revenue. Everyone must also admit that if the municipalities must exercise their functions under the terms of confederation there should also be in existence a system that would tend to preserve Canadian unity, and not a system that would discriminate against a certain group of Canadians because they happen to reside in certain areas where the standard of living and the economic growth is lagging behind, as compared with that of other sections of the country.

FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO CANADIAN PREPARED FOOD EXPORTS
speechtext:
1.	Has the Department of Trade and Commerce been requested to assist a Canadian food manufacturer in Windsor, Ontario, in his efforts to export Chinese-type prepared foods to the United States?
2.	If so: (a) have representations been addressed directly to the minister in this matter by the manufacturer himself or by any body acting on his behalf? (b) has any progress been made in negotiations with the United States government or any of its agencies in this regard? (c) has any agreement yet been reached to permit this Canadian food manufacturer to export his product?
Answer by: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister
of Trade and Commerce):
1.	Yes.
2.	(a) Yes. (b) Yes. (c) Yes. An agreement has now been signed by the Canadian embassy in Washington and the competent U.S. authority. The agreement will take effect when notice of it has been published in the United States federal register. That publication should take place on February 1, enabling the Windsor manufacturer to begin exporting to the United States as of that day.

Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
1.	What is the basis for determining terms and conditions of work for prevailing rate of pay employees in the government service?
2.	What is the role of the prevailing rate advisory committee?
Questions
3.	Who are its members and what are their positions in the federal government service?
4.	Why are prevailing rate of pay employees required to take the first day of sick leave without pay?
5.	During the month of December, did the minister receive representations on behalf of these employees from any staff association?
6.	If so: (a) what association made these representations? (b) does the government contemplate changing its policy in this?
Answer by:	Hon. Donald M. Fleming
(Minister of Finance):
1.	Terms and conditions of work for prevailing rate employees are determined on the basis of information provided by the Department of Labour resulting from surveys of current practices in outside employment.
2.	The prevailing rate advisory committee provides advice to the treasury board on matters pertaining to working conditions of employees under the prevailing rate employees general regulations, ships' officers regulations, and ships' crews regulations.
3.	A. R. K. Anderson, superintendent of civilian personnel, Department of National Defence; J. R. Baxter, director of administration and personnel services, Department of Transport; Charles Caron, treasury board staff; A. Gagnon, treasury board staff; R. J. Groves, director, organization and personnel, Department of Agriculture; J. F. Maxwell, chief, personnel branch, Department of Public Works; K. R. Scobie, director of pay and standards branch, civil service commission; Bernard Wilson, director, industrial relations branch, Department of Labour.
4.	A waiting period for sickness benefits is the current practice in outside employment.
5.	Yes.
6.	(a) The civil service association of Canada. (b) It is not the practice of the government to reveal information on policy matters.
